Hi! My name is…
Greet people, introduce yourself, and ask someone's name, informally (tú) or formally (usted).
Find out how greetings change with the time of day and the situation.

In Spanish, the greeting changes with the time of day and the relationship between the people. This week you learn the basic phrases and the difference between **tú** and **usted**.
Greeting by time of day

To greet anyone at any time, you can say **Hola**. If you want to be more complete or more formal, use the greeting for the time of day: **Buenos días** in the morning, **Buenas tardes** from lunchtime until dark, and **Buenas noches** at night.
It's very common to combine them: **Hola, buenos días**. After the greeting, you ask about the person: **¿Qué tal?** or **¿Cómo estás?**
To say goodbye: **Adiós**, **Hasta luego** (you're leaving but will be back), **Hasta mañana** and, among friends, **Chao** (in Argentina and Uruguay it's written **chau**).
In Argentina and Uruguay you also hear **Buen día** in the morning.
_Tarde_ is feminine: buen**as** tardes.
_Día_ is masculine even though it ends in -a.
Who? Yo, tú, usted, él, ella

Subject pronouns say who does the action: **yo** (the person speaking), **tú** (the person you're talking to, informally), **usted** (the person you're talking to, with respect or distance), **él** and **ella** (another person).

In Spanish the verb already tells you the person. That's why we normally don't say the pronoun: **Soy Ana** is more natural than _Yo soy Ana_. We use the pronoun to contrast or emphasize: **Yo soy Ana y ella es Lucía.**

**Tú or usted.** With friends, family, children, and young people, use **tú**. With an older person you don't know, in an office, or with a client, use **usted**. Careful: _usted_ addresses the person in front of you, but the verb is the same as for _él_ or _ella_: **usted es**.
In Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and much of Central America, **vos** is used instead of _tú_: **vos sos**. This week you only need to recognize it.

There are three common ways to say your name: **Me llamo Marta**, **Soy Marta** and, a bit more formal, **Mi nombre es Marta**.
_Llamarse_ always has a small pronoun in front: **me** llamo, **te** llamas, **se** llama. To ask: **¿Cómo te llamas?** (tú) and **¿Cómo se llama?** or **¿Cómo se llama usted?** (usted).
When someone introduces themselves, reply **Mucho gusto** or **Encantado** (if you're a man) / **Encantada** (if you're a woman). The other person can answer **Igualmente**.
_Llamarse_ needs **me**: me llamo.
The verb goes directly after _cómo_; the pronoun is not needed.

Five vowels, five sounds
Spanish has only **five vowel sounds**: a, e, i, o, u. They are short, clear, and steady: they sound the same at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end of a word, stressed or unstressed.
The big difference from English is that in Spanish **vowels are not reduced**. In _chocolate_ you hear all four full vowels: cho-co-la-te. There's no weak vowel like «uh».
They aren't lengthened or glided either: the **o** in _hola_ doesn't end in «u» and the **e** in _mesa_ doesn't end in «i».
Each vowel is always written with the same letter. The **h** is silent: _hola_ begins with the **o** sound.

The Identities Hub · pronouns

Last week you learned to say who you are. Now you take a step further: **where you're from**, **what languages you speak**, and **how people can contact you**. For that you need the full verb _ser_, the word _no_, nationalities, and the numbers from 0 to 20.
Ser: all the persons
You already know `soy`, `eres`, and `es`. Today you add the plural: **nosotros/nosotras somos**, **vosotros/vosotras sois**, **ustedes son**, and **ellos/ellas son**.

**Nosotros** includes the person speaking and other people: _Camila y yo_ = nosotros. If the group is all women, you say **nosotras**. If there are men and women, the masculine form is used: _nosotros_.

**Vosotros or ustedes.** To address a group, in Spain **vosotros sois** is used with friends and family, and **ustedes son** in formal situations. Throughout Latin America only **ustedes son** is used, for friends and strangers alike. Both forms are correct: pick one according to your variety and recognize the other.
Just like _usted es_, **ustedes son** addresses the people in front of you, but the verb is the same as for _ellos_: **son**.
A trick for the plural: **so-** appears in _somos_, _sois_, and _son_. You only have to change the ending: -mos (nosotros), -is (vosotros), -n (ellos, ustedes).
The verb ser, complete
Person
Pronoun
Example
With _nosotros_ the verb is **somos**.
_Ustedes_ uses the _ellos_ form: **son**. _Sois_ is only for _vosotros_.
Saying no: no + verb
To make a negative in Spanish, put **no before the verb**: _Soy de México_ → **No soy** de México. There are no auxiliary verbs like English _do_ or _does_: just **no**.
If there is a subject pronoun, the order is: subject + **no** + verb: **Ella no es** cubana. With _llamarse_, the **no** goes before _me, te, se_: **No me llamo** Luis.
To answer a question, it's very common to say **no** twice: the first answers, the second negates the verb. —¿Eres española? —**No, no soy** española. Soy chilena.
**No** always goes before the verb.
With _llamarse_, **no** goes before _me_.
Subject + **no** + verb.
Nationalities: masculine, feminine, and plural
Nationalities are adjectives: they change according to the person. There are three main patterns.
**1. Ending in -o:** change the -o to -a. _mexicano → mexicana_, _colombiano → colombiana_.

**2. Ending in a consonant:** add -a. _español → española_, _alemán → alemana_, _francés → francesa_. Careful: the accent mark disappears in the feminine (_inglés → inglesa_), because the word has one more syllable.
**3. Ending in -e or -a:** they are the same for men and women. _estadounidense, canadiense, belga_.
The plural: after a vowel, add **-s** (_mexicanos, canadienses_); after a consonant, **-es** (_españoles, alemanes_). For a mixed group, use the masculine plural: _Ana y Pedro son peruanos_.
In Spanish, nationalities and languages are written in **lowercase**: _Soy francesa. Hablo francés._ Countries are capitalized: _Francia_.

Where are you from? What languages do you speak?

To ask about origin: **¿De dónde eres?** (tú), **¿De dónde es usted?**, **¿De dónde son?** (ustedes). To answer you have two options: **ser de + place** (_Soy de Guadalajara_, _Soy de México_) or **ser + nationality** (_Soy mexicana_). Many people combine both: _Soy mexicana, de Guadalajara_.

For languages use the verb **hablar**: **hablo** (yo), **hablas** (tú), **habla** (él, ella, usted). Question: **¿Qué idiomas hablas?** Answer: _Hablo español e inglés._ If you speak a little: _Hablo un poco de español._
One detail: _y_ becomes **e** before a word that starts with the _i_ sound: español **e** inglés, Francia **e** Italia.
The people of Guadalajara are called **tapatíos** (_tapatío, tapatía_). In Mexico you'll hear: _Soy tapatía_ = I'm from Guadalajara.
A complete, natural answer has three pieces: place + nationality + languages. _Soy de Oporto, soy portugués y hablo portugués e inglés._
In Spanish the preposition goes at the beginning of the question: **De** dónde.
_De_ goes with a place (_de México_); the nationality goes without _de_.
Before the _i_ sound, **y** changes to **e** so the sound isn't repeated.
The numbers from 0 to 20
From 0 to 15 each number has its own word. Memorize especially **once, doce, trece, catorce, quince**: they don't follow _uno, dos, tres_ in a regular way.
From 16 to 19 you say «diez y seis», but it is written as **one single word**: **dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve**. _Dieciséis_ has an accent mark.

To give a phone number, you can say the digits one by one (_tres, tres, uno, cinco…_) or in pairs (_treinta y tres…_). This week use single digits or pairs up to 20. In Spain it's common to group in twos; in Mexico, many people say the number digit by digit or in groups.
Useful question: **¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?** (tú) / **¿Cuál es su número de teléfono?** (usted). Answer: _Es el…_ or just the digits.
From 0 to 20
From 16 to 19 it's written as one word: **dieci**séis.
14 is irregular: **catorce**.

The Spanish syllable: they all weigh the same
Spanish is a language with **syllable-timed rhythm**: each syllable lasts about the same. That's why _Guadalajara_ sounds like a regular row: **gua-da-la-ja-ra**, five equal beats.

The most typical Spanish syllable is **consonant + vowel**: _ca-sa_, _Mé-xi-co_, _pe-ru-a-no_. When there is a consonant between two vowels, it goes with the following vowel: _co-lom-bia-no_, not _col-omb-ia-no_.

When there are two consonants together, they are normally split: _Ar-gen-ti-na_, _es-pa-ñol_. But some pairs are never split: **ch, ll, rr** and combinations with **l** or **r** such as _bl, br, pl, pr, tr, gr_: _Bra-sil_, _in-glés_, _ca-tor-ce_.
The vowels **i** and **u** form a single syllable with another vowel when they are unstressed: Co-lom-**bia**, **die**-ci-séis, **Gua**-da-la-ja-ra, ca-na-**dien**-se. This is called a _diphthong_.

Variation: in the Caribbean, in Andalusia, and in other areas the **s** at the end of a syllable is aspirated or almost disappears: _los dos_ sounds like «loh doh». In central Mexico, in fast speech, some unstressed vowels sound very short. But the basic rule is the same: clear, regular syllables.

To divide words in writing, a consonant between vowels goes with the next vowel (_ca-na-dien-se_). **Ch**, **ll**, and **rr** count as a single letter for syllables: _chi-le-no_, _a-ma-ri-llo_, _pe-rro_.

This week the world fills up with things. To talk about them you need to know whether they are masculine or feminine, how the plural is formed, which article to use, and how to say that something **is** (or **isn't**) in a place. And since you'll come across many new words, you also learn to ask what they mean.
Masculine or feminine
In Spanish **all nouns have gender**: masculine or feminine. For things, gender has nothing to do with sex: _la mesa_ isn't «feminine» in any sense; it's simply grammar.

Often the ending of the word helps you. Words in **-o** are normally masculine: _el libro, el cuaderno, el bolígrafo_. Words in **-a** are normally feminine: _la mesa, la silla, la mochila_. Words in **-ción**, **-sión**, and **-dad** are feminine: _la habitación, la televisión, la ciudad_.

Words in **-e** or in another consonant can be either gender: _el reloj, el lápiz, la llave, la luz, el cine, la calle_. With these words, the only sure strategy is to **learn the word with its article**.

There are some very common exceptions: **el día, el mapa, el problema, el sofá** (masculine in -a) and **la mano, la foto, la moto, la radio** (feminine in -o; _foto_ and _moto_ are short forms of _fotografía_ and _motocicleta_).
For people, many words change like last week's nationalities: _el chico, la chica_. Others are the same and only the article changes: **el estudiante, la estudiante**.

One, two, many: the plural
The rule is very regular. If the word ends in a **vowel**, add **-s**: _libro → libros_, _llave → llaves_, _silla → sillas_.
If it ends in a **consonant**, add **-es**: _reloj → relojes_, _papel → papeles_, _ciudad → ciudades_.
If it ends in **-z**, the z changes to **c** and you add -es: _lápiz → lápices_, _luz → luces_. In Spanish _ze_ or _zi_ is almost never written.

Watch the accent mark: _habitación_ → **habitaciones** (no accent mark), just like _inglés → ingleses_ last week. When you add a syllable, the word no longer needs the accent mark. And the other way around: _joven → jóvenes_ needs a new accent mark.
For a mixed group of people the masculine plural is used, as with nationalities: _el chico + la chica = los chicos_.

The (m./f./pl.) · a, an, some
Articles agree with the noun in gender and number. There are two families. The **definite** ones: **el, la, los, las**. The **indefinite** ones: **un, una, unos, unas**.

**Un / una** introduce something **new** to the listener, or any one of a group: En la mesa hay **un** libro. **El / la** talk about something **known**, already mentioned, or unique in the situation: **El** libro es de Nicolás. We also use _el / la_ for something unique: **la** puerta de la habitación (the room has one door).
_Unos / unas_ means «some, an imprecise amount»: _unas llaves_, _unos cuadernos_. With numbers no indefinite article is used: _dos sillas_, not _unas dos sillas_ (that means «about two»).
Another difference from English: to talk about professions or nationalities with _ser_, _un/una_ is not used: **Soy estudiante**, not _Soy una estudiante_.

Hay: saying what there is in a place
**Hay** says that something **exists** or **is present** in a place. It's one single form for singular and plural: _Hay una cama. Hay dos camas._

After _hay_ you use **un / una / unos / unas**, a **number**, or a **plural noun without an article**: _Hay un clóset_, _Hay tres sillas_, _Hay libros en la mesa_. You don't say _hay el / hay la_: the definite article introduces something already known, and _hay_ introduces something new.
To ask: **¿Hay wifi?** **¿Hay una farmacia aquí?** To negate, **no hay**: _No hay televisión_. With _no hay_ the noun often stands alone, without _un/una_: _No hay toallas. No hay mesa._
Compare _hay_ with _ser_: **Hay una mesa** (a table exists here) / **Es una mesa** (you identify what the object is).
_Hay_ introduces something new: **un / una**, not _el / la_.
_Hay_ doesn't change in the plural.

¿Qué significa…? Asking for clarification
Not understanding is normal, and Spanish has set phrases to sort it out without switching to English. Learn them as blocks:

**¿Qué significa «clóset»?** (you don't know a word) · **¿Cómo se dice «towel» en español?** (you don't know how to say a word) · **¿Cómo se escribe?** (you want to see the word) · **¿Puedes repetir, por favor?** / **¿Puede repetir?** (usted) · **Más despacio, por favor.** · **No entiendo.**
In Mexico you'll hear **¿Mande?** a lot to mean «pardon?, what did you say?». It's very polite. In Spain **¿Perdona?** or **¿Cómo?** is more usual; in almost every country **¿Perdón?** works.

Word stress: one stronger syllable

In every Spanish word there is **one syllable stronger** than the others: the stressed syllable. In _mesa_ it's **me**; in _reloj_ it's **loj**; in _lámpara_ it's **lám**. The strong syllable is a little longer and higher, but the vowel **doesn't change**: all five vowels sound clear in every syllable.
Changing the strong syllable can change the word: **pa**pa (potato, in Latin America _papa_) / pa**pá** (father); **sá**bana (bed sheet) / sa**ba**na (African landscape).

The good news: the accent mark tells you where the stress is when the word doesn't follow the general rule. **Rule 1:** if the word ends in a vowel, **-n**, or **-s**, the strong syllable is the second-to-last: _me-sa, li-bro, si-llas, ha-blan_. **Rule 2:** if it ends in another consonant, it's the last: _re-loj, pa-pel, ciu-dad_. If the word doesn't follow these rules, it takes an accent mark: _lá-piz_, _in-glés_, _ha-bi-ta-ción_, _so-fá_. And if the strong syllable is the third-to-last, it always takes an accent mark: _lám-pa-ra, bo-lí-gra-fo, Mé-xi-co_.

Variation: some words have different stress depending on the country. In Latin America it's _video_ (vi-**de**-o) and in Spain _vídeo_ (**ví**-de-o). In Mexico _chofer_ (cho-**fer**), in Spain _chófer_ (**chó**-fer). The name _Oaxaca_ is pronounced oa-**xa**-ca, and the **x** sounds like **j** (just as in _México_).

The accent mark is written over the vowel of the strong syllable: á, é, í, ó, ú. One-syllable words normally don't take an accent mark (_mes, pan, luz_). On phone keyboards, hold down the vowel to see the accent mark.

Verbs in -ar: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja…

Spanish verbs are divided into three groups according to the infinitive: **-ar**, **-er**, and **-ir**. The biggest group is **-ar**: _trabajar, estudiar, hablar, enseñar, cocinar, escuchar, necesitar, viajar_.

To conjugate a regular -ar verb, remove **-ar** (the stem is left: _trabaj-_) and add the ending for each person: **-o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an**. It's the same pattern you already use with _hablo, hablas, habla_ and with _me llamo, te llamas, se llama_.

Since the ending already tells the person, the subject pronoun normally disappears: **Trabajo en un hospital** (there's no need for _yo_). Use the pronoun to contrast: **Yo** trabajo por la mañana y **ella** trabaja por la noche.
The present tense is used to talk about what you normally do (_Estudio por la tarde_) and also about what is true now in your life (_Trabajo en Monterrey_).
Notice the strong syllable: **tra**-ba-jo, tra-**ba**-jas, tra-ba-**ja**-mos. In _trabajáis_ and _trabajás_ the stress goes at the end, which is why they take an accent mark.

Professions and workplaces
To say your profession use **ser + profession, with no article**: _Soy enfermera._ _Es ingeniero._ The article appears only if you add something more: Es **un** ingeniero muy bueno.

Professions change gender like nationalities. In **-o → -a**: _médico, médica; abogado, abogada; ingeniero, ingeniera; enfermero, enfermera; cocinero, cocinera_. In **consonant → +a**: _profesor, profesora; programador, programadora; diseñador, diseñadora; contador, contadora_. In **-ista** and **-e** they are the same for both: _el/la periodista, el/la recepcionista, el/la estudiante, el/la gerente_.

For the place use **trabajar en + un / una / el / la + place**: _trabajo en un hospital, en una escuela, en la universidad, en una fábrica, en casa_ (without an article). To ask: **¿A qué te dedicas?**, **¿En qué trabajas?**, or **¿Qué estudias?** (with usted: _¿A qué se dedica?_).
There is regional variation: in Mexico it's **mesero / mesera**; in Spain, **camarero / camarera**. In Mexico the accountant is **contador**; in Spain, **contable**.
With _ser_ + profession, _un/una_ is not used.

Asking: qué, dónde, cuándo, cómo, quién, cuánto

Question words **always take an accent mark**: **qué** (thing, information), **dónde** (place), **cuándo** (time), **cómo** (manner), **quién / quiénes** (person), **cuánto / cuánta / cuántos / cuántas** (quantity).

The normal order is: **question word + verb + (subject)**: ¿Dónde trabaja **Ana**? ¿Qué estudian **tus amigos**? If there is a preposition, it goes in front of everything: **¿De dónde** eres? **¿En qué** trabajas? **¿Con quién** trabajas?
**Cuánto** agrees with the noun like an adjective: _¿Cuántas horas trabajas?_ (horas, feminine plural), _¿Cuántos estudiantes hay?_ (masculine plural).

**Yes/no** questions need no question word and don't change the order: _Trabajas en Monterrey._ → _¿Trabajas en Monterrey?_ In writing, the signs **¿ ?** mark the difference; in speech, intonation does.
In the Caribbean (Cuba, Puerto Rico, Dominican Republic) it's normal to hear the subject before the verb: _¿Qué tú estudias?_ It's correct there; in most countries you say _¿Qué estudias (tú)?_

Connecting ideas: y, pero, también
**Y** adds two ideas: Soy ingeniera **y** trabajo en una fábrica. Remember: before the _i_ sound it becomes **e**: español **e** inglés.
**Pero** introduces an idea that contrasts or surprises: Soy médico, **pero** no trabajo en un hospital. Trabajo en una universidad.

**También** adds something equal or of the same kind. It normally goes before the verb or at the end: **También** hablo inglés. / Hablo inglés **también**. To react to another person: —Trabajo en casa. —¡**Yo también**!
With a negative sentence, the reaction is **tampoco**: _—No trabajo los domingos. —Yo tampoco._ For now, just recognize it.

The melody of questions

In Spanish, a yes/no question has **the same words and the same order** as a statement: _Trabajas en Monterrey._ / _¿Trabajas en Monterrey?_ In writing, the signs **¿ ?** mark the question. In speech, only **intonation** marks it.

**Statement:** the voice falls at the end ↘. _Trabajas en Monterrey._ **Yes/no question:** the voice rises at the end ↗. _¿Trabajas en Monterrey?_ If you don't raise your voice, the other person hears a statement.

**Question with qué, dónde, cuándo…:** the question word already says it's a question, so normally the voice **falls** at the end ↘: _¿Dónde trabajas?_ The question word is strong and a little higher. If you rise at the end, the question sounds friendlier or surprised.

That's why **qué, dónde, cómo, cuándo, quién, cuánto** take an accent mark: in questions they are **stressed** (strong) words. Without an accent mark (_que, donde, como, cuando_) they are unstressed words that join sentences: Trabajo **donde** trabaja mi hermana.

Variation: the melody changes a lot between countries. In the Caribbean many yes/no questions end falling; in Buenos Aires the voice rises and falls in a very marked way. But the basic rule, ↗ for yes/no and ↘ for statements, works throughout the Spanish-speaking world.

Questions are written with **¿** at the beginning and **?** at the end; exclamations with **¡ !**. If the question is only part of the sentence, the sign opens where the question begins: _Y tú, ¿dónde trabajas?_

This week there is no new grammar. It's a stop to organize what you already know: with these pieces you can already have your first complete conversation in Spanish. Each summary ends with the most frequent mix-ups at this point in the course.
Ser: your identity card

With **ser** you say who you are: your name (**Soy Nadia**), your origin (**Soy de Malabo**), your nationality (**Soy ecuatoguineana**), and your profession (**Soy diseñadora**). It's the verb of identity.
Origin and nationality say the same thing with two structures: **ser de + place** (soy de Chile) or **ser + adjective** (soy chileno, soy chilena). Don't mix the two: _soy de chilena_ doesn't exist.
With a profession no article is used: **Soy enfermera**, not _soy una enfermera_. The article appears only if you add more information: _Es una enfermera muy buena_.
Remember the plural forms: **somos**, **sois** (vosotros, only in Spain), and **son** (ellos, ellas, ustedes). In Latin America, to address a group, **ustedes** is always used, even among friends.
If you hesitate between _de + country_ and the nationality, use **ser de**: _Soy de Corea_ is always correct, even if you don't remember the adjective.

Things: gender, plural, articles, and hay

All nouns have gender. Many in **-o** are masculine (el libro) and many in **-a** are feminine (la mesa), but there are frequent exceptions: **el día**, **el mapa**, **el idioma**, **el problema**, **la mano**, **la foto**. Words in **-e** or in a consonant must be learned with their article: **la clase**, **el lápiz**.
Plural: vowel + **-s** (mesa → mesas), consonant + **-es** (papel → papeles), and **z → ces** (lápiz → lápices).
**El, la, los, las** talk about something known or unique: _el teléfono de Rocío_. **Un, una, unos, unas** introduce something new: _un teléfono_.

**Hay** says that something exists in a place. It's one single form for singular and plural, and goes with **un/una**, with numbers, or without an article: _Hay una impresora_, _Hay doce mesas_, _Hay café_. It never goes with _el, la, los, las_.
Ordenador (Spain) and computadora (Latin America) are the same thing. Use the word from the region you prefer, but recognize both.

-ar verbs, negation, and questions

To talk about what you do, you use regular verbs in **-ar**: you remove **-ar** and add the ending for the person: habl**o**, habl**as**, habl**a**, habl**amos**, habl**áis**, habl**an**. It's the same with trabajar, estudiar, dedicarse, necesitar, or escuchar.

To negate, put **no** right before the verb: **No hablo francés**. If you answer a question, there are often two _no_: **—¿Trabajas aquí? —No, no trabajo aquí.** The first answers; the second negates the verb.

Question words take an accent mark: **qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, quién, cuánto**. They go at the beginning, right before the verb: **¿Dónde trabajas?** In yes/no questions there's no special word: the intonation rises at the end: **¿Hablas inglés?**

Connecting ideas and saying numbers

An introduction sounds natural when the sentences are connected: **y** adds (hablo inglés **y** francés), **pero** contrasts (soy ingeniera, **pero** ahora estudio diseño), and **también** adds something equal (Pau es estudiante; Nadia **también**).
Before a word that begins with the sound **i**, _y_ changes to **e**: **español e inglés**.
Numbers: from 16 to 29 they are written as one word (**dieciséis, veintidós, veintiocho**); from 31 on they are written as three (**treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco**). **Cien** is exactly 100.

Phone numbers are often said in groups of two digits: 99 23 45 80 → **noventa y nueve, veintitrés, cuarenta y cinco, ochenta**. If you don't understand, ask for clarification: **¿Cómo? Más despacio, por favor.**
To sound natural in an introduction, use at least one **pero** and one **también**: they are the difference between a list and a text.

Review: vowels, syllables, stress, and intonation

The four weeks of pronunciation form a system. There are five **vowels** and they are always clear. Each **syllable** has about the same duration: Spanish sounds like a regular train, ta-ta-ta-ta. One of those syllables is stronger: the **stress**. And the **intonation** of the sentence says whether you are asking or stating.

If you change the stress, you sometimes change the word: **trabajo** (yo, now) versus **trabajó** (in the past, you'll see it later). And if you change the intonation, you change the message: **Eres de Chile.** (you state) versus **¿Eres de Chile?** (you ask, the voice rises at the end).
In questions with **qué, dónde, cómo**, the voice normally falls at the end: the question word already says it's a question.
The written accent mark marks the strong syllable when it doesn't follow the general rule (**teléfono**, **lápiz**) and also distinguishes the question words: **¿dónde?** versus _donde_.

Talking about family is one of the first topics in any conversation. To do it you need three tools: the verb **tener**, **possessives**, and **adjectives** that describe.
Tener: family, age, and appearance

**Tener** is a very frequent irregular verb. This week you use it for three things: family (**Tengo dos hermanas**), age (**Mi abuela tiene ochenta años**), and some physical features (**Tiene el pelo rizado**, **Tiene los ojos verdes**).
Watch out for age: in Spanish you don't _be_ an age, you _have_ it. **Tengo treinta años**, not _soy treinta_. To ask: **¿Cuántos años tienes?** (tú) or **¿Cuántos años tiene usted?**

In negative sentences and general questions, the noun often goes without an article: **No tengo hijos.** **¿Tienes hermanos?** It's like with _hay_: we are talking about existence, not a specific person.
The forms of **yo** (tengo) and of **tú, él, ellos** (tienes, tiene, tienen) are irregular; **nosotros** and **vosotros** are regular. With **vos** it's **tenés**.
Answer _¿Cuántos años tienes?_ with the number alone (**Veintiséis**) or with the full sentence (**Tengo veintiséis años**). Both are natural.

Mi, tu, su, nuestro: whose is it?
Possessives go before the noun and say whose it is: **mi madre**, **tu primo**, **su hermana**.
They agree with the thing or person possessed, not with the possessor. That's why one person says **mis padres** (two parents) and two people say **nuestra abuela** (one grandmother, feminine).
**Mi, tu, su** only change in number (mi/mis). **Nuestro** and **vuestro** change in gender and number: nuestro tío, nuestra tía, nuestros tíos, nuestras tías.
**Su** can mean his, her, your (usted), their (ellos, ellas), or your (ustedes). If it's not clear, clarify with **de** + person: _la casa de ella_, _el hermano de usted_.
Don't confuse **tu** (possessive, no accent mark: _tu hermano_) with **tú** (pronoun, with an accent mark: _¿Tú tienes hermanos?_).

Describing a person: agreeing adjectives
To describe appearance and personality you use **ser + adjective**: _Mi tía es alta y simpática._ The adjective agrees in gender and number with the person.

Adjectives in **-o**: four forms (alto, alta, altos, altas). Adjectives in **-e** or in a consonant: one form for masculine and feminine, and plural with -s or -es (inteligente/inteligentes, joven/jóvenes). Adjectives in **-or** add **-a** in the feminine: trabajador → trabajadora.
For a mixed group of men and women, the adjective goes in the **masculine plural**: _Mis abuelos son simpáticos_ (the grandfather and the grandmother).
For hair and eyes, use **tener**: _Tiene el pelo largo y liso._ For a person's hair color you can also use **ser**: _Es rubio_, _Es morena_.
Regional variation: in Mexico they say **güero/güera** for _rubio/rubia_ and **ojos cafés** for _ojos marrones_; in Argentina and Uruguay, **morocho/morocha** for _moreno/morena_.
To avoid sounding negative, soften: **un poco** + negative adjective (_es un poco serio_) and **muy** + positive adjective (_es muy amable_).

The family: who's who

Family words almost always have a form in **-o** for men and one in **-a** for women: hermano/hermana, tío/tía, primo/prima, abuelo/abuela. Exceptions: **padre/madre**, **marido/mujer**, **yerno/nuera**.
The **masculine plural** is used for a mixed group: **mis padres** = my father and my mother; **mis hermanos** can be only boys or boys and girls. If they are only girls: **mis hermanas**.
To explain relationships, use **de**: _La hermana de mi madre es mi tía. El hijo de mi tía es mi primo._

In everyday conversation you hear **mamá** and **papá**, and in Argentina and Uruguay **mis viejos** (affectionately) for parents. For a married couple: **esposo/esposa** (very common in Latin America) or **marido/mujer** (very common in Spain).
_Parientes_ = relatives (the whole family). _Padres_ = father and mother.

C, Z, and S: seseo and distinción
The letter **c** has two sounds. Before **a, o, u** it sounds **[k]**: **ca**sa, **co**sa, **cu**ñado. Before **e, i** it has the same sound as **z**: **ce**na, **ci**nco, **za**pato, a**zu**l.

That sound of **ce, ci, za, zo, zu** is pronounced in two ways, and both are correct. In most of Spain the **distinción** is used: a **[θ]** sound, like the English _th_ in _think_, different from the **s**. In Latin America, the Canary Islands, and much of Andalusia the **seseo** is used: **ce, ci, z** sound exactly like **s**.

With seseo, _casa_ and _caza_ sound the same; with distinción, they're different. Choose one system and be consistent; what matters is **recognizing both**. (In some areas of Andalusia there's also **ceceo**: all the **s** sounds are pronounced as [θ].)

The **s** always sounds [s], throughout the Spanish-speaking world, although in many areas of the Caribbean, Andalusia, and the Southern Cone it's aspirated at the end of a syllable: _do**s** primo**s**_ → «doh primoh».
We write **z** before a, o, u (_zapato, zorro, azul_) and **c** before e, i (_cena, cinco_). That's why plurals change: _lápiz → lápices_, _feliz → felices_, _vez → veces_.

You already conjugate **-ar** verbs (week 4). This week you complete the regular present-tense system with **-er** and **-ir** verbs, and learn to say how often you do things: the basis for talking about your habits.
Verbs in -er and -ir: almost the same
The system is the same as for -ar: you remove **-er** or **-ir** and add the ending. The typical vowel now is **e**: com**o**, com**es**, com**e**, com**en**.
Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** differ only in **nosotros** and **vosotros**: com**emos** / viv**imos**, com**éis** / viv**ís**. In all other persons they are the same: com**e** / viv**e**.
Frequent -er verbs: **comer, beber, leer, aprender, vender, comprender, correr**. -ir verbs: **vivir, escribir, compartir, abrir, recibir, subir**.
With **vos** the ending takes an accent mark: **vos comés**, **vos vivís**. In Latin America, **beber** is used, but for drinks **tomar** (an -ar verb) is very common: _¿Qué tomas?_
Three patterns of the regular present
Person
In nosotros, -ir verbs end in **-imos**.
The ella form has no accent mark: **come**. The accent mark is for _vos comés_.

How often?
To say how many times you do something, use a scale: **siempre** → **casi siempre** → **normalmente** → **a menudo / muchas veces** → **a veces** → **casi nunca** → **nunca**.
You can also be exact: **todos los días**, **todas las mañanas**, **una vez a la semana**, **dos veces al mes**. Notice the agreement: tod**os** los días, tod**as** las mañanas.

Most of these expressions go before the verb or at the end of the sentence: **Siempre desayuno café** / **Desayuno café siempre**. **Todos los días** and **una vez a la semana** usually go at the end or at the beginning: **Como fruta todos los días.**

**Nunca** has a special rule. Before the verb it stands alone: **Nunca bebo café.** After the verb it needs **no** in front: **No bebo nunca café.** This is the double negative: in Spanish it is correct and required.
A short answer is also natural: —¿Bebes café? —**Nunca.** / —**A veces.** There's no need to repeat the verb.

The meals of the day and their names

In almost the whole Spanish-speaking world there are three main meals: **desayuno** (in the morning), **comida** or **almuerzo** (at midday or in the afternoon), and **cena** (at night). The verbs are regular -ar verbs: **desayunar**, **cenar**.

The names change by country. In many Latin American countries, **el almuerzo** is the midday meal. In Spain **la comida** is more usual. In Mexico, **la comida** is the main meal of the afternoon and **el almuerzo** can be a late breakfast, in mid-morning.

Many foods have regional variants: **jugo** (Latin America) / **zumo** (Spain); **papa** (Latin America, Canary Islands) / **patata** (Spain); **frijoles** (Mexico, Central America) / **porotos** (Southern Cone) / **caraotas** (Venezuela). Careful: a **torta** in Mexico is a sandwich; in other countries, a sweet cake.
_Desayunar_ and _cenar_ already include the time: **desayuno café**, **ceno sopa**.

B and V: a single sound

In modern Spanish, **b** and **v** are pronounced exactly the same. _Vino_ and _bino_ would sound identical: the difference is only in spelling. Don't pronounce the **v** with your teeth on your lip, as in English.

That single sound has two variants depending on position. After a pause and after **m** or **n**, the lips close completely: it's a **strong [b]**, as in _**V**ino, por favor_, _u**n v**aso_, _ta**mb**ién_.
In other positions —especially between vowels— the lips almost touch, but don't close: it's a **soft [β]**, as in _la **v**erdura_, _be**b**o_, _Cu**b**a_. The air passes between the lips.
What matters: the variant depends on the **position**, not on the letter. The same word changes: _**v**aso_ (strong, at the beginning) → _el **v**aso_ (soft).

Since they sound the same, **b** and **v** are learned with the written word. Two clues: after **m** it's always written **b** (_también, hambre_) and after **n** always **v** (_invitar, enviar_). The past-tense endings **-aba** and words with **bl, br** take **b**.

Estar: where is it?
To say **where** a person, thing, or place is, Spanish uses the verb **estar**, not _ser_. **El banco está en la plaza.** **Estoy en el hotel.** **¿Dónde estás?**

_Estar_ is irregular in the **yo** form (`estoy`, like `soy`) and takes an accent mark in almost all the others: `estás`, `está`, `están`. The accent mark shows where the stress goes: es-**TÁ**, not **ES**-ta (_esta_ without an accent mark is another word: _esta calle_).

The key question is **¿Dónde está…?** (one place) or **¿Dónde están…?** (several places). In Guatemala, Argentina, and other countries with **vos**, the form is the same as with tú: **¿Dónde estás vos?**
Remember the rhyme: **cómo estás y dónde estás** always go with _estar_.

Hay or está?
You already know **hay** (week 3): it's used to say that something **exists** in a place. Now you need to choose between **hay** and **está**, and the rule depends on the word that comes after.

Use **hay** when you introduce something **new** or non-specific: **hay** + _un, una, unos, unas_, + number (_dos, tres_…), + _mucho, muchos_… or + noun without an article. **¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?** **Hay dos bancos en esta calle.** **No hay cajero.**

Use **está / están** when you talk about something **known** and specific: + _el, la, los, las_, + _mi, tu, su_…, + proper names. **¿Dónde está la farmacia?** **Mi hotel está cerca.** **El Mercado Central está detrás de la catedral.**
Notice: _hay_ never changes (one thing or many: **hay**). _Estar_ agrees with what is located: **la plaza está**, **las tiendas están**.
Quick trick: if in English you say _there is / there are_, in Spanish it's almost always **hay**.

Cerca de, al lado de, enfrente de… and the forms al and del

To locate one place relative to another, use these expressions. Almost all end in **de**: **cerca de**, **lejos de**, **al lado de**, **enfrente de**, **delante de**, **detrás de**, **a la derecha de**, **a la izquierda de**. **Entre** goes without _de_: **entre el banco y la iglesia**. And for inside a place: **en** (en la plaza, en la zona 1, en la esquina).

When **de** meets **el**, they merge: **de + el = del**. The same happens with **a + el = al**. It's mandatory: **al lado del banco** (not _al lado de el banco_). With _la, los, las_ there is no merging: **al lado de la farmacia**, **cerca de los mercados**.
The contraction doesn't happen with the pronoun **él** (with an accent mark): _al lado de él_. Nor in names that have _El_ capitalized: _Soy de El Salvador_.

The single r and the strong rr
Spanish has **two r sounds**. The **single r** is a quick tap of the tip of the tongue behind the upper teeth, very similar to the _t_ in American English _water_: **pero**, **caro**, **para**.

The **strong rr** (multiple trill) is two, three, or more taps in a row: the tongue vibrates with the air. Changing one for the other changes the word: **pero** (_but_) / **perro** (_dog_), **caro** (_expensive_) / **carro** (_car_), **cero** (_zero_) / **cerro** (_hill_).

When does it sound strong? Whenever **rr** is written (only between vowels: _perro, carro_), at the **beginning of a word** (_Roma, rojo, restaurante_), and after **n, l, s** (_Enrique, alrededor, Israel_). In other cases the **r** is single.

Real variation: in Guatemala, Costa Rica, and parts of the Andes, the rr and the final r can sound with a friction, like _zh_ (assibilated rr). In Puerto Rico it is sometimes heard further back, in the throat. Both are normal variants. To learn, first work on the clear tap of the tongue.
The double **rr** is only written between vowels (_perro, barrio, correo_). At the beginning of a word or after n, l, s a single **r** is written, but it sounds strong: _Roma, Enrique, alrededor_.
single r (one tap)
strong rr (several taps)
Why strong?
One light tap, like the quick _t_ in _water_. The tongue touches and leaves.

_Perdón, farmacia, por_: single r before a consonant or at the end. A short tap, without the English r.

A routine is a chain of actions with times: **me levanto a las siete, desayuno, trabajo…** This week you learn the three pieces you need: reflexive verbs, the time, and the days.
Me levanto, te duchas, se acuesta: reflexive verbs

Many routine actions are **reflexive**: the person who does the action also receives it. **Me ducho** = I shower myself. In the dictionary, these verbs end in **-se**: _levantarse_, _ducharse_, _lavarse_, _acostarse_.

They are conjugated like any verb, but with a pronoun in front that changes with the person: **me, te, se, nos, os, se**. The pronoun goes **before** the conjugated verb and separate: **me levanto**, **nos duchamos**. With negation, the _no_ goes in front of everything: **No me levanto temprano.**

Compare: **Lavo el carro** (the action goes to the car) and **Me lavo las manos** (the action comes back to me). With body parts we use the article, not the possessive: **me lavo los dientes**, not _mis dientes_.

Two very frequent verbs change the stem vowel: **despertarse** → `me despierto` and **acostarse** → `me acuesto`. This week learn them as blocks: **me despierto, te despiertas, se despierta**; **me acuesto, te acuestas, se acuesta** (but _nos despertamos_, _nos acostamos_). In week 11 you'll see the full pattern.
Trick: when you learn a routine verb, learn it with its pronoun: not _levantar_, but **me levanto**.

What time is it? At what time…?
To ask the time: **¿Qué hora es?** To answer we use _ser_ + **la** (one) or **las** (the others): **Es la una.** **Son las tres.** The word _horas_ isn't said: it's hidden in _la_ and _las_.

For minutes: **y** + minutes up to the half hour (**y cinco, y cuarto, y media**) and **menos** + minutes after (**las ocho menos cuarto** = 7:45). In Mexico and Central America you also hear **un cuarto para las ocho** or **quince para las ocho**. For the exact hour: **en punto**.

To say **when** something happens, we don't use _es / son_ but **a**: **¿A qué hora te levantas?** — **A las siete.** **A la una.** To specify: **de la mañana**, **de la tarde**, **de la noche**. At 12:00 noon it's **mediodía**; at 00:00, **medianoche**.
In written schedules (trains, stores, classes) the 24-hour clock is used a lot: _17:30_. When speaking, people normally say **las cinco y media de la tarde**.

Days and parts of the day
The days of the week are masculine and written in **lowercase**: **lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo**. Saturday and Sunday make up **el fin de semana**.

With days, _en_ is not used. **El lunes** = this Monday, one time. **Los lunes** = every Monday, a habit. Compare: **El lunes tengo una cita.** / **Los lunes tengo clase de yoga.** For a period: **de lunes a viernes**.

The parts of the day change a bit by country: **por la mañana** (Spain and many countries), **en la mañana** (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), **a la mañana** (Argentina, Uruguay). The same with _la tarde_ and _la noche_. All are correct.
Notice the first letters: **l, m, m, j, v, s, d**. That's how the days appear on many Hispanic calendars.
With days the article **el / los** is used, not _en_.

Telling your day in order

For your routine to be understood, put the actions in order with sequence connectors: **primero**, **después**, **luego**, **más tarde**, and **por último** (or **al final**). To join two actions, use what you already know: **y**, **pero**, **también**.

A simple structure for telling a day: **time + action**. _A las siete me levanto. Después me ducho y desayuno. A las ocho y media empiezo a trabajar…_ There's no need to repeat the subject: the verb already says who.
To ask about another person's routine: **¿A qué hora te levantas?**, **¿Qué haces por la mañana?**, **¿Trabajas los sábados?** With usted: **¿A qué hora se levanta usted?**
Vary the connectors: **después**, **luego**, **más tarde**. Always repeating the same one sounds like a list.

The jota and the g: gente, gato, guitarra

The **jota** is a sound that English doesn't have in its normal words: air passes with friction at the back of the mouth, between the tongue and the soft palate, like when you breathe out to clean glasses, but stronger. It's always written **j** (_jamón, ajo, jueves, José_) and **g** before **e, i** (_gente, girasol, página_).

Before **a, o, u** and before a consonant, the **g** is soft, as in English _go_: **gato, gol, gusto, Guatemala, grande**. To have that soft sound before _e, i_, **gu** is written and the _u_ is silent: **guerra, guitarra, seguimos**. If the _u_ is pronounced, it takes a diaeresis: _pingüino_.
Between vowels, the soft g is even more relaxed: in _agua_ or _lago_ the tongue barely touches the palate.

Variation: in northern and central Spain the jota is strong and rough. In much of Latin America, including Guatemala, and in Andalusia and the Canary Islands, the jota is much softer, almost like the English _h_ in _house_. Both are understood everywhere. What matters is **not** to pronounce it like the English _j_ in _jam_.
Same sound, two letters: _ja, jo, ju_ always with **j**; _je, ji_ sometimes with **j** (_jefe, jirafa_) and sometimes with **g** (_gente, girasol_). For a soft sound before e, i: **gue, gui**.

My name is Ana Lucía and I'm a tour guide in Antigua Guatemala. Many people ask me: «¿Cómo es un día normal para ti?». Here is my Monday.

I wake up at five thirty. Yes, very early! First I get up and shower; then I have breakfast with my sister: coffee, pan dulce, and fruit. At a quarter past six I walk to the Plaza Mayor. On Mondays there is a group for the Pacaya volcano and the bus leaves at a quarter to seven.

At night I have dinner with my sister, read for a while, and go to bed at ten. On Tuesday, five thirty again! But on Saturdays and Sundays I don't work: I get up at nine and never look at the clock.

Ser, estar, tener, and hay: four verbs, four jobs

To describe people and places you need four verbs, and each has its own job. **Ser** says what or how someone or something is: identity, origin, profession, personality, appearance (**Mi hermana es alta y muy simpática**).

**Estar** says where someone or something is (**Mi casa está cerca del lago**). **Tener** says what a person has: family, age, things, features (**Tengo dos hermanos**, **Mi abuelo tiene ochenta años**, **Tiene el pelo corto**). **Hay** says what exists in a place, with new information (**En mi barrio hay un mercado**).
The question that helps you choose: **cómo es**? → ser; **dónde está**? → estar; **qué tiene** / **cuántos años tiene**? → tener; **qué hay** there? → hay.
When you describe someone, use all three: **es** (what they're like), **tiene** (what they have), and **está** (where they are now). It sounds complete and natural.

Mi, tu, su… and agreement

The possessives **mi, tu, su** agree in number with the thing possessed, not with the person: **mi hermano**, **mis hermanos**. **Nuestro** and **vuestro** also agree in gender: **nuestra casa**, **nuestros padres**.
**Su** has many possible owners: his, her, your (usted), their (ellos, ellas), your (ustedes). If it's not clear, clarify with **de** + person: **la casa de él**, **la casa de Ana**.

Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun: **un tío alto**, **una tía alta**, **unos primos altos**. Those ending in **-e** or a consonant don't change in the feminine: **una hermana inteligente**, **una amiga joven** (but **jóvenes** in the plural). Also remember nationalities: **español → española**.

The present tense of your week: -ar, -er, -ir, and reflexive

Your whole day fits in the present tense. **-ar** verbs have **-a-** in the endings (_trabajo, trabajas, trabaja_…); **-er** and **-ir** verbs have **-e-** (_como, comes, come; vivo, vives, vive_), and only separate in nosotros and vosotros: **comemos / vivimos**, **coméis / vivís**.
Reflexive verbs are the same, but with **me, te, se, nos, os, se** in front: **me levanto**, **nos acostamos**. Remember the blocks with vowel change: **me despierto**, **me acuesto**.

To talk about habits, add frequency: **siempre**, **casi siempre**, **normalmente**, **a veces**, **casi nunca**, **nunca**. With _nunca_ there are two positions: **Nunca como carne** or **No como carne nunca**. And to place the action in time: **a las ocho**, **los lunes**, **por la mañana**.
The time of an action goes with **a**: _a las ocho_; the time right now, with **es / son**: _son las ocho_.

Listening to a voice message

A voice message almost always has the same shape: **greeting** (_¡Hola! Soy Mateo_), **reason** (_te llamo por lo del sábado_), **details** (place, time, who), and **goodbye** (_¡Nos vemos!_, _Un beso_). If you know this shape, you know where the important information is: in the middle.

Before listening, prepare three questions: **¿Dónde?**, **¿A qué hora?**, and **¿Qué plan?** While listening, don't try to understand everything: note only numbers, times, place names, and the prepositions that go with them (_enfrente de, detrás de_…).

Listen twice. The first time, to know who is speaking and why. The second, to complete your notes. Watch for changes of plan: words like **pero**, **no**, or **mejor** announce that something changes.
If the message gives two times, the last one you hear after **pero** or **mejor** is usually the right one.
Translating everything makes you lose the important details. Look only for the answers to your three questions.

Review: c/z/s, b/v, r/rr, and the jota

In these four weeks you have worked on four difficult points. **C, Z, and S**: in almost all of Latin America and in parts of Andalusia and the Canary Islands, _casa_ and _caza_ sound the same (**seseo**); in central and northern Spain, _ce, ci, za, zo, zu_ sound like the _th_ in _think_ (**distinción**). Both are correct.

**B and V** are the same sound throughout the Spanish-speaking world: _vaca_ and _baca_ are pronounced the same. At the beginning of a sentence or after _m, n_ the lips close (_un vaso_); between vowels they barely touch (_la vaca, el lobo_).

**R and RR**: one tap (_pero, caro_) or several (_perro, carro, Roma, Enrique_). **J and G**: _jueves, gente_ with jota; _gato, guitarra_ with soft g. In Guatemala the jota is soft, almost an aspirated _h_.
This week you put the four sounds together in real sentences about family, places, and routine. Go slowly first and then at normal speed.

Four writing rules: **z** before a, o, u and **c** before e, i (_zapato, cine_); **b** or **v** are learned with the word (_vivir, beber_); **rr** only between vowels; **j** always with a, o, u (_jamón, joven, jugo_) and **g** or **j** before e, i (_gente, jefe_).

This week you're in San Salvador. Your friends write to you: «¿Querés subir al volcán el sábado?». To reply you need very common verbs that change a vowel: **querer**, **poder**, **preferir**, **jugar**…
Verbs that change the vowel: e → ie, o → ue, u → ue, e → i

Some verbs change the last vowel of the stem when that syllable is **stressed**. _Querer_ → **quie**ro; _poder_ → **pue**do; _jugar_ → **jue**go; _pedir_ → **pi**do. The endings are the usual ones (-o, -es, -e, -emos…).

Why only in some persons? Because in **nosotros** and **vosotros** the stress moves to the ending: que-**re**-mos, po-**de**-mos. The stem is no longer stressed and doesn't change. That's why people talk about the "shoe" or "boot" pattern: if you draw the table and mark the forms that change, it looks like a boot.

There are four groups. **e → ie**: querer, preferir, empezar, entender, pensar, cerrar. **o → ue**: poder, volver, dormir, almorzar, costar, encontrar. **u → ue**: only _jugar_. **e → i** (only -ir verbs): pedir, repetir, servir.
The dictionary doesn't warn you. That's why it's a good idea to learn these verbs with a label: _querer (ie)_, _poder (ue)_, _pedir (i)_.
Quick trick: if the **nosotros** form is regular and the **yo** form changes, you have a "boot" verb. Always practice out loud: qu**ie**ro, qu**ie**res, qu**ie**re, queremos.
The "boot" pattern: the forms that change are in bold
_Poder_ changes **o → ue** in the stressed syllable: p**ue**do.
With _nosotros_ the stem isn't stressed, so it doesn't change: **queremos**.
_Jugar_ changes **u → ue**: j**ue**go, j**ue**gas, j**ue**ga.
Querer, poder, and preferir + infinitive

With **querer** you say what you want, with **poder** what is possible for you, and with **preferir** what you choose between two options. All three can go with an **infinitive**: the second verb is not conjugated.

The structure is simple: conjugated verb + infinitive. **Quiero ver** a movie. **¿Puedes jugar** on Saturday? **Prefiero nadar** in the pool. There is no word between the two verbs: not _a_, not _de_, not _que_.

If the infinitive is reflexive (levantarse, acostarse, ducharse), the pronoun goes **attached to the end** of the infinitive or **before the first verb**: _Quiero levantar**me** tarde_ = _**Me** quiero levantar tarde_. Both forms are correct.
To say you can't, add a reason: _No puedo, **es que** trabajo el sábado_. **Es que** introduces an explanation and sounds kinder.
After _querer_ the second verb is in the **infinitive**: _ir_.
Between _poder_ and the infinitive there is no preposition.
_Levantarse_ is reflexive: the pronoun **me** doesn't disappear.
Vos querés, vos podés: voseo in Central America

In El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Costa Rica, many people use **vos** with friends and family, just like in Argentina and Uruguay. In this course you learn **tú** as the main form, but you will hear _vos_ on the street and in messages.

The good news: with **vos** these verbs **don't change the vowel**. The form looks like the infinitive and has an accent mark at the end: querer → **vos querés**, poder → **vos podés**, jugar → **vos jugás**, preferir → **vos preferís**, pedir → **vos pedís**.
The same happens with regular verbs: **vos trabajás**, **vos comés**, **vos vivís**. With reflexive verbs, the pronoun is **te**: _¿A qué hora te levantás?_
Tú and vos mean the same thing. In San Salvador you also hear **usted** among friends and in the family: it's a way of showing affection and respect, not distance.
If you hear a form with an accent mark at the end and no vowel change (_podés, jugás_), it's almost certainly **vos**.

Suggesting, accepting, and saying no

To **suggest** something to a person, use a question with _querer_ or _poder_: **¿Quieres jugar al fútbol?** **¿Puedes el sábado?** To suggest something we do together, use **¿Por qué no…?** + a verb in _nosotros_: **¿Por qué no comemos pupusas?**

To **accept**: **¡Sí, claro!**, **¡Buena idea!**, **¡Perfecto!** Each region has its own quick word: **¡Va, pues!** in El Salvador and Honduras, **¡Dale!** in Central America and the Río de la Plata, **¡Vale!** in Spain, **¡Sale!** or **¡Va!** in Mexico.

To **say no** politely, there are three steps: express regret (**Lo siento**), explain (**es que…**), and suggest something else (**¿Y el domingo?**, **Prefiero…**). A bare _no_ without an explanation sounds abrupt in Spanish.
To wrap up the plan, confirm the day, the time, and the place: _Entonces, el sábado a las ocho. ¿Dónde **está** el parque?_

Ñ, LL, and Y

The **ñ** is a letter of its own in Spanish. To pronounce it, press the middle of your tongue against the hard palate and let the air out through your nose. It is similar to the _ny_ in _canyon_, but it is **a single sound**: _ma-ña-na_, not _man-ya-na_.
**N** and **ñ** tell words apart: _cana_ (white hair) and _caña_ (cane), _pena_ and _peña_, _mono_ and _moño_. If you don't separate them, you change the meaning.

**LL** and **Y**: in most of the Spanish-speaking world they sound the same (this phenomenon is called **yeísmo**). _Calle_ and _cayó_, _pollo_ and _poyo_ have the same sound, similar to the _y_ in _yes_ but a little stronger.

Real variation: in Buenos Aires and Montevideo, **ll** and **y** sound like the _sh_ in _show_ or the _s_ in _vision_: _yo me shamo_. In the relaxed speech of El Salvador and Honduras, the **ll** between vowels can sound very soft or almost disappear: _ga(y)ina_, _sía_ for _silla_. All of these pronunciations are correct in their region.

The **ñ** is always written with a tilde: if you don't have a Spanish keyboard, don't replace it with _n_ or _ny_. **Ll** and **y** sound the same for many people, so you have to learn the spelling word by word: _calle_, _playa_. At the end of a word, the _i_ sound is written **y**: _hoy, muy, soy_.

In Tegucigalpa, on the university radio, they ask students: «¿Qué te gusta hacer?». To answer in Spanish you need a verb that works the opposite way from English: **gustar**.
Gustar: the thing that is liked is the subject

In English you say _I like music_: the person is the subject. In Spanish the idea is "music is pleasing **to me**": the **thing** is the subject and the person appears as a pronoun: **me, te, le, nos, os, les**.

That's why the verb agrees with the thing, not with the person. One thing or one activity: **gusta**. Several things: **gustan**. _Me gusta **la salsa**._ _Me gustan **las series**._ _Nos gusta **bailar**._
With infinitives you always use **gusta**, even if there are two or three activities: _Me gusta leer y cantar_.
Things normally take an article: _Me gusta **el** café_, _Te gustan **los** perros_. You are talking about the thing in general, so the article is not omitted.
To clarify or emphasize, add **a + person**: _**A Carlos** le gusta el rock_, _**A mí** me encanta_, _¿**A ti** te gusta?_ With vos (Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador…): _¿**A vos** te gusta?_
To avoid mistakes, look for the thing: if it's plural, add **-n**. The person never changes the verb.

Muy and mucho
**Muy** goes before an adjective or an adverb and never changes: _muy interesante_, _muy divertidas_, _muy bien_, _muy temprano_.

**Mucho** has two uses. After a verb it doesn't change: _Me gusta **mucho**_, _Leo **mucho**_, _Duermo **mucho** los domingos_. Before a noun it agrees with it like an adjective: **mucho** tiempo, **mucha** música, **muchos** libros, **muchas** series.
A simple question helps: what word comes next? Adjective or adverb → **muy**. Noun → **mucho/a/os/as**. Nothing (or the end of the sentence) after a verb → **mucho**.
They are never said together: _muy mucho_ doesn't exist. And _muy_ can't go alone at the end of a sentence.

Silent H, CH, and the /k/ sound (c, qu, k)

The **h** is never pronounced in Spanish: _hola_ sounds like "ola," _hermano_ like "ermano," _ahora_ like "aora." It's a letter that exists only in writing. Don't pronounce it like the English _h_ of _house_: that sound in Spanish is written with **j**.

The **ch** is a single sound, like the _ch_ in _church_: _mucho_, _ocho_, _chocolate_, _noche_. In some areas of Andalusia, Chile, and northern Mexico it sounds softer, close to _sh_: _musho_ for _mucho_.

The /k/ sound is written three ways. With **c** before a, o, u: _casa, comer, cuatro_. With **qu** before e, i: _queso, quince, ¿qué?, ¿quién?_. In _qu_, the **u is silent**: _queso_ is "keso." With **k** only in words from other languages: _kilo, kiwi, karaoke_.
Careful: **c** before **e, i** is not /k/: _cine, cena_ sound with /s/ in Latin America and the Canary Islands, or with /θ/ in much of Spain.

Golden rule: the /k/ sound is **ca, que, qui, co, cu**. That's why _queso_, not _keso_; _cuatro_, not _quatro_. You have to learn **h** word by word because it's silent: _hora_ (time) and _ora_ (prays) sound the same.

In Granada, Nicaragua, the streets of the center are full of clothing, hat, and craft shops. To shop you need to point things out (_esta camisa_, _aquel sombrero_), understand prices in córdobas, and ask for what you want politely.
Este, ese, aquel: pointing according to distance
Demonstratives point to a thing and say **how far away** it is. **Este** = near me (here). **Ese** = near you or at a medium distance (there). **Aquel** = far from both of us (over there).

They agree in gender and number with the noun, like an adjective, but they go **before** it: _est**a** camisa_, _es**os** pantalones_, _aquell**as** sandalias_. Notice that the masculine singular is irregular: **este**, **ese**, **aquel** (not _esto_, _eso_, _aquello_).
If the noun is already clear, you can use the demonstrative alone: _—¿Qué camisa te gusta? —**Esta**._ Today it is written without an accent mark.

Variation: in Latin America, in everyday conversation, many people also use **ese** for faraway things, and **aquel** is heard less. In Spain all three distances are used a lot. Both options are correct.
To remember: each demonstrative has its adverb of place. **este** → _aquí_, **ese** → _ahí_, **aquel** → _allí_. _Aquel_ and _allí_ are the longest words, like the distance.

Esto, eso, aquello: when you don't know the name
**Esto**, **eso**, and **aquello** are neuter forms: they have no feminine or plural and **never** go with a noun.
They are used for things whose name you don't know (_¿Qué es **esto**?_), for a group of things (_¿Cuánto cuesta todo **esto**?_), and for ideas or situations (_**Eso** es muy caro_; _¡**Eso** es!_).
Compare: _¿Qué es **esto**?_ (I don't know what it is) and _¿Cuánto cuesta **este**?_ (I already know it's a hat and I'm pointing at it).
If you don't know what the thing is, you don't know its gender: use the neuter **esto**.
Numbers from one hundred: prices and quantities

**Cien** is exactly 100: _cien córdobas_, _cien mil_. From 101 you say **ciento**: _ciento uno_, _ciento cincuenta_, _ciento noventa y nueve_. Never _ciento y…_: the **y** only goes between the tens and the ones (_treinta **y** cinco_).
The hundreds from 200 to 900 **agree** with the noun: _doscient**os** córdobas_, _doscient**as** camisas_. Three are irregular: **quinientos** (500), **setecientos** (700), and **novecientos** (900).
**Mil** doesn't change: _mil_, _dos mil_, _diez mil_ (never _dos miles_). **Un millón** does have a plural and takes **de** before a noun: _dos millones de personas_.
To read a price, say the thousands first and then the rest: 1250 = _mil doscientos cincuenta_; 2499 = _dos mil cuatrocientos noventa y nueve_.

Currencies on this route: in Nicaragua, the **córdoba** (C$); in Honduras, the **lempira**; in El Salvador, the **dollar**. When writing large numbers, each country uses a period, comma, or space to separate thousands; the Royal Academy recommends a space (_12 500_) or nothing in four-digit numbers (_1250_).

Clothes and colors

The color goes **after** the noun and agrees with it: _una falda roj**a**_, _unos pantalones negr**os**_. Colors ending in **-o** have four forms: rojo, roja, rojos, rojas (also negro, blanco, amarillo).
Colors ending in **-e** or a consonant have only singular and plural: _una camisa verde_, _unos tenis verdes_; _un suéter azul_, _unas sandalias azules_; _gris → grises_, _marrón → marrones_.
**Rosa** and **naranja** normally don't change: _unos zapatos rosa_, _una gorra naranja_. For any color you can say _de color_ + color: _una camisa de color naranja_.

Clothing names change by country. _Camiseta_ (Spain, Central America) is _playera_ in Mexico and _remera_ in Argentina. _Chaqueta_ is _chamarra_ in Mexico and _campera_ in Argentina. Sports shoes are _tenis_ in Mexico and Central America. And brown is _café_ in much of Latin America.
For clothes you ask about the **size**: _¿Qué talla usa?_ (Latin America), _¿Qué talla tiene?_ (Spain). Sizes are usually S, M, L or pequeña, mediana, grande.
The color goes **after** the noun.
_Azul_ has a plural: **azules**.
_Negro_ ends in -o: it has a feminine, **negra**.
In the store: asking, trying on, and deciding
To ask the price: **¿Cuánto cuesta** este sombrero? (one thing) / **¿Cuánto cuestan** estos tenis? (several). _Costar_ is a "boot" verb: c**ue**sta. In Central America you also hear **¿Cuánto vale?**
To ask for another option: **¿Tiene esta camisa en azul?** **¿Tiene una talla más grande?** **¿Hay en talla M?**
To try on clothes you use the reflexive **probarse** (o → ue): _Me pruebo la camisa_; _¿Puedo probarme estos pantalones?_ And you ask: _¿Dónde **están** los probadores?_
After trying something on, use **quedar**, which works like _gustar_: **me queda** bien / grande / pequeño (one thing), **me quedan** grandes (several things): _Los pantalones me quedan pequeños_.

To decide: **Me llevo** esta / este / estos. If you don't want anything: _Gracias, solo estoy mirando_. To pay: **¿Aceptan tarjeta?** or _Pago en efectivo_. In Nicaraguan markets you can ask for a discount: _¿Me hace un descuento?_
With salespeople you normally use **usted**: _¿Tiene…?_, _¿Me hace…?_ In Nicaragua you will hear **vos** among friends (_¿Vos qué talla usás?_), but in stores _usted_ is the most normal.
The most useful question of the week: **¿Cuánto cuesta este?** + a pointing finger. If you don't understand the number, ask: _¿Puede escribir el precio, por favor?_

The soft d

The Spanish **d** has two versions. At the beginning of a sentence and after **n** or **l**, it is a **hard d**: the tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and closes off the air. _¡Dos!_, _tienda_, _falda_, _cuando_.

In other positions, especially **between vowels**, it is a **soft d** [ð]: the tongue approaches the teeth **without closing**, and the air passes. It sounds similar to the English _th_ of _this_, but weaker. _Todo_, _vestido_, _cada_, _verde_, _nada_.

The soft d is very important in shopping: _vestido, todo, ¿cuánto es todo?, pagado, mercado_. If you pronounce it hard like in English, it sounds foreign; if you pronounce it like an English _r_, _todo_ sounds like _toro_.

Real variation: in the fast speech of Spain and the Caribbean, the d of **-ado** almost disappears: _cansao_ for _cansado_, _el mercao_. And the **final d** (_ciudad, usted, Madrid_) is very weak or not heard at all in many regions. For study, pronounce the soft d, but don't be surprised if you hear it dropped.
The letter is always **d**: the sound changes because of position, not spelling. Don't write _-ao_ for _-ado_: _cansao_ only appears in very informal messages or in texts that imitate speech.

This week you are in **León, Nicaragua**, a university city with many cheap, good eateries. To eat well in Spanish you need three things: phrases for ordering, words of quantity, and a few very common verbs that are irregular only in **yo**.
Ordering at a restaurant: polite phrases

Many restaurants in Latin America and Spain have a **menú del día**: a fixed price with a **first course** (de primero), a **second course** (de segundo), **dessert**, and sometimes a **drink**. If you want to see all the dishes, you ask for **la carta** (in Latin America it is also called **el menú**).

With the waiter you normally use **usted**. The most useful phrases are: **Para mí, la sopa**; **De primero, la ensalada, y de segundo, el pollo**; **¿Me trae un agua, por favor?**; **¿Me puede traer otra servilleta?**; **¿Qué me recomienda?**

To ask about a dish: **¿El arroz lleva carne?** (_llevar_ = to have as an ingredient), **¿Es picante?** For a change: **Sin cebolla, por favor.** At the end: **La cuenta, por favor** or **¿Nos trae la cuenta?** And if you want to know how to pay: **¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?**
The waiter also uses set phrases: **¿Qué quieren tomar?** (to drink), **¿Algo más?**, **Ahora le traigo la cuenta.** In _le traigo_, **le** means _a usted_: learn it as a block.

**Variation.** The person who serves is called **mesero/mesera** in Mexico and Central America, **camarero/camarera** in Spain, **mozo/moza** in Argentina and Uruguay, and **mesonero/mesonera** in Venezuela. In Central America, a **fresco** is a natural fruit or cocoa drink (in Mexico, _agua fresca_; in other countries, _jugo_ or _zumo_).
You say **un agua** and **el agua**, even though _agua_ is feminine (_el agua fría_). This happens with feminine words that begin with a stressed **a**.

How much? Poco, un poco de, bastante, demasiado, nada de
You already know **mucho** and **muy**. Now you complete the scale of quantity: **nada de** → **poco** → **un poco de** → **bastante** → **mucho** → **demasiado**.

**Before a noun**, _poco_, _mucho_, and _demasiado_ agree with it: **poca sal**, **pocos turistas**, **demasiada gente**, **demasiados platos**. _Bastante_ only changes in the plural: **bastante arroz**, **bastantes mesas**. _Un poco de_ doesn't change: **un poco de pan**, **un poco de agua**.

**Before an adjective or after a verb**, they never change: **La sopa es bastante picante**, **El café es demasiado dulce**, **Como poco**. For adjectives use **un poco** without _de_: **un poco caro**.

**Poco** and **un poco** don't mean the same thing. _Hay poca sopa_ is negative: it's not enough. _Hay un poco de sopa_ is positive: there is some. And **demasiado** always means "more than needed": _demasiado picante_ is a problem, _muy picante_ is just a description.
**Nada de** works like _nunca_: if it comes after the verb, you need **no** before it: **No tiene nada de carne.**
Trick: if you can put _muy_, use the form that doesn't change (_bastante caro_, _demasiado caro_). If you can put _mucho/mucha_, use the form that agrees (_demasiada sal_).

Some very common verbs are **irregular only in the yo form**. The other persons are regular: _hago_, but **haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen**.

**The -go group**: hacer → **hago**, poner → **pongo**, traer → **traigo**, salir → **salgo**. **The -zco group**: conocer → **conozco**. **Just one**: saber → **sé** (with an accent mark, so you don't confuse it with the pronoun _se_ of _se llama_).

**Conocer or saber.** **Conocer** is having experience with a place, a dish, or a thing: _Conozco León_, _¿Conoces el quesillo?_. **Saber** is having information or a skill: _No sé el precio_, _¿Sabes dónde está el mercado?_, _Sé cocinar_ (saber + infinitive).

These verbs appear a lot at the restaurant and in routines: **Salgo** to dinner on Fridays, **pongo** the table, **traigo** the dessert, **hago** dinner, **no sé** what to order, **conozco** a very good eatery.

Diphthongs and hiatuses: bue-no, pe-dí-a… and Le-ón

Spanish vowels are **strong** (a, e, o) or **weak** (i, u). When an unstressed weak vowel goes next to another vowel, the two form **a single syllable**: it's a **diphthong**. _Bue-no_, _ciu-dad_, _cuen-ta_, _a-gua_, _sie-te_.

Two strong vowels together go in **separate syllables**: it's a **hiatus**. _Le-ón_, _te-a-tro_, _pa-se-o_. There is also a hiatus when the weak vowel carries the stress: then it takes an **accent mark**: _dí-a_, _pa-ís_, _frí-o_, _Ma-rí-a_.

You already know many diphthongs: verbs with vowel change create them. _Quiero_, _pienso_, _puedo_, _cuesta_, _recomienda_: the **ie** and the **ue** are pronounced together, in a single beat of voice.

In the fast, familiar speech of many countries (Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, Andalusia), some hiatuses become diphthongs: _teatro_ sounds almost like "tia-tro" and _pelear_ almost like "pe-liar". It's normal on the street, but to start, pronounce the full hiatus.
The accent mark on **í** or **ú** always indicates a hiatus: _día_, _país_, _Raúl_. Without an accent mark, _i_ and _u_ next to another vowel form a diphthong: _piano_, _ciudad_.

This is a **checkpoint**: there is no new grammar. Here you organize what you already know and clear up the most typical confusions. The stop is **San José, Costa Rica**, where many people use **usted** even with friends and family (the _ustedeo_), and also **vos** among friends. That's why this week usted appears in very informal situations.
Two types of irregular verbs

**Type 1: vowel change** (week 11). The stem vowel changes in **yo, tú, él/ella/usted, and ellos/ustedes**, but **not** in nosotros or vosotros: **quiero**, quieres, quiere, **queremos**, queréis, quieren. The changes are **e → ie** (querer, preferir, pensar, empezar, recomendar), **o → ue** (poder, costar, dormir, volver), **u → ue** (jugar), and **e → i** (pedir, servir, repetir).
**Type 2: irregular yo** (week 14). Only the **yo** form changes: **hago**, haces; **salgo**, sales; **pongo**, **traigo**, **conozco**, **sé**. Everything else is regular.
**Tener** mixes both types: **tengo** (yo with -go) and **tienes, tiene, tienen** (e → ie), but **tenemos**.

**Querer, poder, and preferir + infinitive** go directly with the infinitive, without a preposition: **Quiero comer en una soda**, **¿Puede venir el sábado?**, **Prefiero comprar ropa en el mercado**.
If you're unsure, think of **nosotros**: if the nosotros form is regular (_podemos, queremos, pedimos_), the verb probably has a vowel change.

Likes and reactions: gustar, querer, también and tampoco

With **gustar**, the thing that is liked decides the verb: **me gusta** + one thing or an infinitive (_me gusta el teatro_, _me gusta bailar_) and **me gustan** + several things (_me gustan las sodas_). The same with **encantar** and **interesar**. In front go **me, te, le, nos, os, les**.

**Gustar or querer.** _Me gusta el teatro_ talks about your likes in general. _Quiero ir al teatro_ talks about a specific wish, right now. To suggest a plan you use **querer**: _¿Quieres ir al teatro el sábado?_

**Reacting.** If the other person says something **positive** (_Me encanta el fútbol_), you reply **A mí también** (same) or **A mí no** (different). If they say something **negative** (_No me gusta el ruido_), you reply **A mí tampoco** (same) or **A mí sí** (different).

In Costa Rica, among friends, you often hear **¿A usted le gusta…?** and **¿Usted quiere…?**: it's the Costa Rican ustedeo, and it is neither cold nor distant. Among friends **vos** is also used: _¿Vos querés venir?_

I think the same
I think differently
With gustar: **me** + gustan (agrees with _los conciertos_).
To agree with a negative sentence: **tampoco**.
_Encantar_ already means "to like a lot": it doesn't need _mucho_.
How much? Muy, mucho, and the scale of quantity

**Muy** goes with adjectives and adverbs and never changes: **muy barato**, **muy cerca**. **Mucho** goes with nouns and agrees (**mucha** gente, **muchos** turistas) or goes with verbs and doesn't change (_me gusta **mucho**_, _trabaja **mucho**_).

The quantifiers from week 14 follow the same logic: before a noun they agree (**poca** sal, **demasiadas** tiendas, **bastantes** mesas); with an adjective or a verb they don't change (**demasiado** caras, **un poco** caro, como **bastante**).

The full scale: **nada de** → **poco** → **un poco de** → **bastante** → **mucho** → **demasiado**. Remember: _poco_ is negative (_hay poca comida_: it's not enough) and _un poco de_ is positive (_hay un poco de comida_: there is some).

Pointing, shopping, and ordering

**Este, ese, aquel** agree with the noun and tell the distance: **esta** camiseta (here, near me), **esa** gorra (there, near you), **aquellos** zapatos (over there, far from both). **Esto** and **eso** don't change and are for things without a name: _¿Qué es eso?_

In the **store** and at the **restaurant** you use parallel phrases. To ask the price: _¿Cuánto cuesta esta camisa?_ / _¿Cuánto es?_ To choose: _Me llevo esta_ / _Para mí, el casado_. To ask for something: _¿Tiene una talla más grande?_ / _¿Me trae un fresco?_ To pay: _¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?_ in both places.

**In Costa Rica** prices are in **colones** (₡): a casado costs about **₡3500** (tres mil quinientos colones). A **soda** is a small, family-run, cheap restaurant. And when you say _gracias_, people often reply **Con mucho gusto**.
In Costa Rica, _¡Pura vida!_ is used to greet, say goodbye, say thank you, and say that everything is fine.

Sound review: ñ, ll/y, h, ch, soft d, and diphthongs

In weeks 11 to 14 you worked on five points. **Ñ**: the tongue touches the palate, as in _año_ or _mañana_; it is not _n_ + _i_. **LL and Y**: in almost all of the Spanish-speaking world they sound the same (yeísmo); in Argentina and Uruguay they sound like "sh" or "zh."
**H**: it is never pronounced: _hola_ = "ola." **CH** sounds like English _church_. The **k** sound is written **c** (ca, co, cu), **qu** (que, qui), and sometimes **k**: _casa, queso, kilo_.
**Soft D**: between vowels, the **d** is very soft, almost like _th_ in _this_: _todo, moda, nada_. In the fast speech of many areas the **d** of **-ado** almost disappears: _pescao_ for _pescado_.

**Diphthongs**: _bue-no, cuen-ta, vein-te_ in one syllable; **hiatuses**: _dí-a, pa-ís, Le-ón_ in two. In Costa Rica, by the way, the **r** of many people sounds a bit like the English _r_: it's not a mistake, it's regional variation.
Summary of letters: **ñ** always sounds the same; **ll** and **y** almost always the same; **h** never sounds; the **k** sound = c (a, o, u) / qu (e, i); the accent mark on **í, ú** marks a hiatus.

To talk about **plans** and **intentions** we use the verb **ir** in the present + **a** + **infinitive**: **Voy a visitar** a coffee farm. **¿Qué vas a hacer** on Saturday? **Vamos a cruzar** the hanging bridges.

The verb **ir** is very irregular: **voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van**. With **vos** it's the same as with tú: _vos vas_. Only **ir** changes; the second verb is always in the infinitive: _vamos a **cenar**_, never _vamos a cenamos_.

**Querer, poder, or ir a.** _Quiero hacer canopy_ is a wish. _Puedo hacer canopy_ is a possibility. _Voy a hacer canopy_ is a decided plan. To negate, **no** goes before _ir_: **No voy a salir esta noche.**

**Ir a + place** also exists and has no infinitive: _Voy a Monteverde_ (destination). You can combine the two: **Voy a ir a Monteverde.** And **¡Vamos a…!** is used to suggest: _¡Vamos a comer!_ = _Let's eat!_
In Costa Rica, with the ustedeo, among friends you hear: **¿Usted qué va a hacer mañana, mae?**

When? Future markers

Plans need a time. From today toward the future: **hoy**, **esta mañana**, **esta tarde**, **esta noche** → **mañana** (por la mañana, por la tarde…) → **pasado mañana** → **el sábado**, **este fin de semana** → **la semana que viene** / **la próxima semana** → **el mes que viene** → **este verano**, **el año que viene**.
**Dentro de** + amount of time says how much time remains from now: **dentro de dos días**, **dentro de una semana**. In Latin America you also hear _en dos días_ with the same meaning.

With days of the week you do **not** use _en_: **el sábado** (this Saturday), **los sábados** (every Saturday). The markers can go at the beginning or the end: _Mañana voy a madrugar_ / _Voy a madrugar mañana_.

Watch out for seasons: in Costa Rica **verano** (summer) is the dry season (December to April) and **invierno** (winter) is the rainy season (May to November). It doesn't depend on cold, it depends on rain.
**Mañana** has two meanings: _mañana_ = tomorrow and _la mañana_ = the morning. That's why **mañana por la mañana** exists: tomorrow morning.

For the weather there are four structures. **Hace** + noun: _hace calor, hace frío, hace sol, hace viento, hace buen tiempo, hace mal tiempo_. **Verbs alone**: _llueve_ (llover, o → ue), _nieva_. **Hay** + noun: _hay niebla, hay nubes, hay viento, hay una tormenta_. **Está** + adjective: _está nublado_.

Since _calor_, _frío_, and _viento_ are nouns, you use **mucho**, not _muy_: **hace mucho calor**, **hace mucho frío**, **hay mucha niebla**. But _nublado_ is an adjective: **está muy nublado**. The same happens with quantifiers: **demasiado frío**, **poco viento**, **bastante lluvia**.

For the future, use **ir a**: **va a llover**, **va a hacer frío**, **va a estar nublado**, **va a haber niebla** (from _hay_). The temperature: **Hace 18 grados** or, very commonly, **Estamos a 18 grados**.

**Transportation.** You go **en** + vehicle: _en bus, en carro, en tren, en avión, en taxi, en bici, en barco_. But you go **a pie** and **a caballo**. The names change by country: the **autobús** (Spain) is **bus** in Costa Rica and Colombia, **camión** in Mexico, **colectivo** in Argentina, and **guagua** in Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Canary Islands. Spain's **coche** is **carro** in almost all of Latin America and **auto** in Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay.
