Linking: los_amigos, van_a_ir

In Spanish we don't speak word by word: we join the words of a sentence. When a word ends in a **consonant** and the next one begins with a **vowel**, the consonant moves to the next syllable: _los amigos_ sounds **lo-sa-mi-gos**; _es un hotel_ sounds **e-su-no-tel**.
Remember that the **h** is silent: _un hotel_ starts the link with the **o**: **u-no-tel**. The same in _mis hermanos_: **mi-ser-ma-nos**.

This is very important with **ir a**: _van a ir_ sounds **va-na-ir**; _vamos a hacer_ sounds **va-mo-sa-ha-cer** (with the silent h: **va-mo-sa-cer**). If you pause between words, you sound like a robot.

In the Caribbean, in Andalusia, and in parts of Central America, the final **s** is aspirated: _los amigos_ sounds almost like "loh amigoh." The linking still exists, but with a soft sound like an English _h_.
Linking doesn't change spelling: you write _los amigos_ with a space, but you say it like one word. Hearing the linking well helps you separate words when you listen to native speakers.

To describe a house in Spanish you need three verbs: **hay**, **estar**, and **ser**. They are not interchangeable: each one answers a different question. This week you learn to choose well, and to use **estar** for states: tired, happy, dirty, open…
Hay, estar, and ser: three questions, three verbs

**Hay** answers the question _¿qué hay?_ (what is there?): it introduces something for the first time, it says it exists. **Hay dos dormitorios. Hay un balcón. No hay ascensor.** After _hay_ comes a number, **un / una / unos / unas**, or a noun without an article. Never _el_ or _la_.

**Estar** answers _¿dónde está?_ (where is it?): it gives the location of something we already know. That's why it takes **el, la, mi, tu…** before it: **El apartamento está en el centro. La cocina está al lado de la sala. Mi cuarto está en el segundo piso.**

**Ser** answers _¿cómo es?_ (what is it like?): it describes the characteristics that are part of the thing. **El apartamento es grande. Es moderno. Es de alquiler.** It is also used to identify: **Esta es la cocina.**
A natural description uses all three verbs together: **Mi casa está en un barrio tranquilo. Es pequeña, pero es muy bonita. Hay una sala, una cocina y dos cuartos.**
Look at the article: **un / una** or a number → almost always _hay_; **el / la / mi** + place → almost always _está_.

With **estar** + adjective we say the **state** of a person or thing at a specific moment: **Estoy cansada. Estamos contentos. La cocina está sucia. La farmacia está cerrada.**

With **ser** + adjective we say what something is normally like: its characteristic. Compare: **La cocina es pequeña** (always, it's its size) and **La cocina está sucia** (today; tomorrow it may be clean).
The adjective agrees with the person or thing in gender and number: **La ventana está abierta. Los cuartos están ordenados. Ana y Luz están cansadas.**
Very useful state adjectives. For people: **cansado, contento, nervioso, enfermo, aburrido, ocupado**. For things and places: **limpio, sucio, ordenado, desordenado, abierto, cerrado, roto, libre**.

Parts of the house and floors

Words for the house change by country. A dwelling in a building is a **piso** in Spain, an **apartamento** in Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, or the Caribbean, and a **departamento** in Mexico, Argentina, Chile, or Peru. The room for sleeping is the **dormitorio**, the **habitación**, or the **cuarto**; in Mexico, also the **recámara**. The living room is the **salón** in Spain and the **sala** in Latin America.

For the number of the floor we use ordinals: **primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto, sexto, séptimo, octavo, noveno, décimo**. Before a masculine noun, _primero_ and _tercero_ lose the **-o**: **el primer piso, el tercer piso**. With a feminine noun they agree: **la primera planta, la tercera puerta**.

Careful: in Spain, the street level is the **planta baja** and the **primer piso** is above it. In many Latin American countries, the **primer piso** is the street level. When you are not sure, ask: **¿Es el piso de la calle?**

Rhythm and synalepha: la_amiga, mi_hijo

Last week you linked consonant + vowel (los_amigos). This week we link **vowel + vowel**. When a word ends in a vowel and the next one begins with a vowel, the two vowels go in the **same syllable**. It's called **sinalefa** (synalepha): _la amiga_ doesn't sound "la · a-mi-ga," but **la_a-mi-ga**, with three beats.
The **h** is silent, so there is also synalepha in **mi_hijo**, **la_habitación**, **su_hermano**: the vowels touch.

If the two vowels are the same, they almost merge into one, a little longer: **está_abierta**, **la_amiga**. If they are different, you go from one to the other without stopping: **mi_apartamento**, **todo_está**.
That's why Spanish sounds so continuous: within a sentence there are no pauses between words, and each syllable lasts about the same. If you separate each word, your Spanish sounds slow and choppy.

In Caribbean speech, also in Panama, the final **-s** is often aspirated or disappears (_los amigos_ → "loh amigo"). That's why even more vowels appear together there. You don't need to imitate it, but it's good to recognize it.
Synalepha is not written: the space between words is still there, but you don't hear it. The initial **h** is also silent, so it doesn't prevent the link: _la_habitación_.

This week you talk about obligations: what **you have to** do, what **one has to** do in general, and what **you need**. You also learn a very useful way to avoid repeating words: **lo, la, los, las**.
Tener que, hay que, and necesitar

**Tener que + infinitive** expresses an obligation of a specific person. The verb _tener_ changes with the person: **Tengo que limpiar el baño. ¿Tienes que trabajar el sábado? Mis hermanos tienen que estudiar.**

**Hay que + infinitive** expresses a general obligation, for everyone, without saying who. _Hay que_ never changes and has no subject: **En esta casa hay que sacar la basura los martes. Hay que pedir cita para renovar el pasaporte.**
**Necesitar** expresses need. It goes with an infinitive or a noun, without a preposition: **Necesito comprar pan. Necesitamos una escoba nueva.**
The three forms combine with the time markers you already know: **Mañana tengo que ir al banco. Esta semana hay que limpiar la terraza.**
Ask yourself: is it a rule for everyone (_en esta casa…_, _en el trabajo…_)? → **hay que**. Is it my obligation or yours? → **tengo que / tienes que**.

Lo, la, los, las: not repeating

When a thing is already in the conversation, we don't repeat it: we use **lo, la, los, las**. The pronoun agrees with the word it replaces: **el pan → lo**, **la basura → la**, **los platos → los**, **las plantas → las**.
With a conjugated verb, the pronoun goes **before** the verb: **—¿Quién compra el pan? —Lo compro yo. —¿Y las plantas? —Las riego yo.**

With an infinitive (after _tener que_, _ir a_, _hay que_…), you have two options: **before the conjugated verb** or **attached to the end of the infinitive**: **La tengo que limpiar** = **Tengo que limpiarla**. **Los voy a lavar** = **Voy a lavarlos.** Both are correct and common.
With _hay que_ there is only one option: attached to the infinitive. **¿La cocina? Hay que limpiarla.**
When you attach the pronoun to the infinitive, the stress stays in the same place: _lim**piar**lo, com**prar**la_. It doesn't need an accent mark.

The personal a
When the direct object is a specific **person**, we put **a** in front: **Llamo a mi madre. Visito a mis abuelos. Ayudo a Carmen con la mudanza.** With things, no: **Llamo un taxi. Visito el museo.**
Remember the contraction: **a + el = al**. **Llamo al plomero** (Latin America) / **al fontanero** (Spain).
To replace a person we also use **lo, la, los, las**: **—¿Ves a Diego hoy? —Sí, lo veo en la cena. —¿Y a las niñas? —Las llevo yo al colegio.**
In Spain many people use **le** for a man: _A Diego le veo mañana_. It's normal to hear it; you can use **lo**, which is understood everywhere.
_Mi abuela_ is a specific person: it needs **a**.
A taxi is a thing (a service): without **a**.
Organizing tasks: who does what?
To share out tasks, ask **¿Quién…?** and answer with the pronoun and the subject at the end: **—¿Quién hace la cena? —La hago yo.** Putting _yo_ at the end is very natural when you offer.
To talk about turns, use **tocar**: **Hoy me toca a mí. ¿A quién le toca sacar la basura? Te toca a ti.** It's the same in Spain and in Latin America.
To give tasks to a group, remember: in Spain **vosotros tenéis que…**; in Latin America **ustedes tienen que…**. To ask politely: **¿Puedes lavar los platos?** (tú) / **¿Puede usted…?** (usted).
A to-do list in Spanish usually uses the infinitive: _Comprar pan. Sacar la basura. Llamar al dueño._

Consonant clusters: tr, pr, pl, bl, cr, gr

Many Spanish words have two consonants together before the vowel: **tr**es, **pl**ato, ha**bl**ar, o**tr**o, **gr**ande, **cr**ema, **pr**imo. The two consonants go **in the same syllable**: o-**tro**, ha-**blar**, li-**bro**.
The golden rule: **don't add a vowel** in the middle. _Tres_ has one syllable, not two ("te-res"). _Plato_ has two, not three ("pe-la-to").
The **r** inside the cluster is always **single**, the short r of _pero_: a single quick tap of the tongue. Don't make the strong rr of _perro_ in _tres_ or _otro_.
The **l** of the cluster is clear, with the tip of the tongue behind the upper teeth: **pl**aya, **bl**anco, **cl**ase.

Variation: in Chile and in parts of Costa Rica and the Andes, the **tr** cluster sometimes sounds almost like **ch**: _otro_ can sound similar to "ocho." It's a normal variant; you can use the general tr.
When dividing syllables, the cluster is never broken: _o-tro_, _ha-blar_, _ne-gro_, _li-bro_. That's why, if a word doesn't fit at the end of the line, it is cut like this: _ha-_ / _blar_.

Celebrating is a huge part of social life in Spanish. To take part you need three things: clear **dates**, **phrases** for inviting and replying, and a good **excuse** for when you can't go.
Dates: el 21 de octubre

In Spanish the date goes in this order: **el + number + de + month**: **el 21 de octubre**, **el 3 de mayo**. If you add the year: **el 3 de mayo de 2027** (_dos mil veintisiete_). If you add the day of the week, it goes first: **el sábado 17 de octubre**.
To ask: **¿Qué día es hoy?** → **Hoy es lunes, 12 de octubre.** **¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños?** → **Es el 9 de julio.** In Spain you also hear **¿A cuántos estamos?** → **Estamos a 12.**

The 1st: in Latin America people almost always say **el primero de mayo**; in Spain **el uno de mayo** is very normal. Both are understood everywhere. The other days use normal numbers: _el dos, el tres, el veinte…_
Months are written in **lowercase**: _enero, julio, diciembre_. And when we write the date with numbers, the day comes **first**: **9/7** is the 9th of July, not the 7th of September.
With months alone we use **en**: **Mi cumpleaños es en julio.** With a specific date we use **el**: **Mi cumpleaños es el 9 de julio.**

*Seasons depend on the hemisphere: in Argentina or Chile, December is summer. In Panama, near the equator, people talk more about **la temporada seca** (the dry season, roughly December to April) and **la temporada de lluvias** (the rainy season).

Many holidays have a fixed date (_Navidad es el 25 de diciembre_) and others change every year: _el Día de la Madre es el segundo domingo de mayo_ in many countries, but not in all.
For the day of the month we use the normal number. Only the 1st can be _primero_.
Why? Because… It's that…
**¿Por qué?** (two words, with an accent mark) asks the reason: **¿Por qué estás tan contenta?** **Porque** (one word, no accent mark) gives the reason: **Porque mañana es mi cumpleaños.**

**Es que…** also explains, but it has another use: presenting an **excuse** or justifying yourself gently. It is the most natural way to say no to an invitation: **—¿Vienes a la cena? —Ay, lo siento, es que tengo que trabajar.**

Why isn't _porque_ enough? Compare: **No voy porque no quiero** (direct, it can sound harsh) and **Lo siento, es que tengo mucho trabajo** (kind). With _es que_ the other person understands that you would like to go.
**¿Por qué no…?** is also used to suggest: **¿Por qué no hacemos una fiesta sorpresa?**

**Inviting.** The simplest way is a question with _querer_: **¿Quieres venir a mi fiesta?** Also: **¿Vienes a cenar el sábado?**, **Te invito a mi cumpleaños**. In Spain you often hear **¿Te apetece…?**; in many Latin American countries, **¿Te animas a…?**. With vos: **¿Querés venir?**
**Accepting with enthusiasm.** **¡Claro! ¡Qué buena idea! ¡Me encanta! ¡Genial!** And a very useful question: **¿Llevo algo?**

**Declining kindly.** Follow four steps: thank → regret → explain with _es que_ → suggest something else. **Gracias por la invitación. ¡Qué pena! Es que ese día tengo que trabajar. ¿Quedamos otro día?**

**A complete invitation** says what, when, where, and what to bring: **El sábado 17 voy a hacer una fiesta. Es a las ocho, en mi casa. Tienes que traer algo para beber.** Careful: an event _es_ at a place (**la fiesta es en mi casa**), but a thing _está_ at a place (**mi casa está en el centro**).
If you can't go, always say something nice about the plan: **¡Qué buena idea! Es que…**. It sounds much better than starting with _no_.

What a surprise! Exclamatory intonation and lists

In week 4 you saw that the yes-or-no question **rises** at the end and the statement **falls**. The exclamation is a third melody: it **starts high**, puts a lot of force on the important word, and **falls** clearly at the end: **¡Qué sorpresa!**, **¡Felicidades!**, **¡Es tu cumpleaños!**

Compare three sentences with the same words: _Es tu cumpleaños._ (information, medium tone, falls) · _¿Es tu cumpleaños?_ (question, rises at the end) · _¡Es tu cumpleaños!_ (surprise or joy: higher, more energy, falls at the end).

In exclamations with **qué** (_¡Qué bonito!, ¡Qué pena!, ¡Qué buena idea!_), _qué_ and the stressed syllable of the adjective are the two peaks. Don't say them in a flat tone: in Spanish, an exclamation without energy sounds boring or ironic.

In a **list**, each item ends a bit high, as if saying "there's more"; only the **last** one, after _y_, falls: _Hay música ↗, comida ↗, bebidas ↗ y un pastel ↘._ If you fall earlier, the other person thinks the list is over.

The melody changes by country: in the Río de la Plata the stressed syllable is stretched a lot; in the Caribbean, also in Panama, the voice rises and falls with more movement. But the basic pattern (high energy and a falling end) is understood everywhere.

In Spanish the exclamation is written with two marks: **¡** at the beginning and **!** at the end. The opening one warns the reader from the first word which melody to use. Exclamatory **qué** takes an accent mark: _¡Qué bonito!_

Ser, estar, hay… and hace: the complete map

You now have four verbs to describe the world. **Ser** says what something is like or what it is (_la casa es antigua_) and also where and when an event is (_la fiesta es en mi casa, es a las ocho_). **Estar** says where a known thing is (_la casa está en el centro_) and how something is right now (_estoy cansada, la puerta está abierta_). **Hay** introduces something new (_hay un balcón_).

For the weather, **hace** and **está** are added: **hace calor, hace frío, hace sol, hace viento** (also **hay viento**); **está nublado, está despejado**; and the weather verbs **llueve** and **nieva**.

The most frequent confusion in A1 is using _ser_ for states (_soy cansado_) or _estar_ for events (_la fiesta está en…_). If in doubt, ask the question: what is it like? where is it? what is there? how is it today? where is the party?

Plans, obligations, and wishes

Three structures with an infinitive cover almost all of the A1 future. **Ir a + infinitive** = a plan or an intention: _voy a viajar_. **Tener que / hay que + infinitive** = an obligation: _tengo que trabajar_, _hay que reservar_. **Querer / poder / preferir + infinitive** = wish, possibility, preference: _quiero descansar_, _no puedo ir_.

All of them combine with future markers: **mañana, pasado mañana, el fin de semana que viene, la semana que viene, este verano, dentro de dos semanas**. The marker can go at the beginning or the end: _Este verano voy a aprender a nadar_ = _Voy a aprender a nadar este verano_.
Together they let you talk about your real schedule: **El sábado quiero ir a la playa, pero no puedo: tengo que estudiar. Voy a ir el domingo.**

Lo, la, los, las and the personal a
To avoid repeating a thing or a person already known, use **lo, la, los, las**, with the gender and number of the word: _el billete → lo_, _la cámara → la_, _los vasos → los_, _las fotos → las_.

The position is the big trap: **before the conjugated verb** (_lo compro_), or **attached to the infinitive** (_voy a comprarlo_, _tengo que comprarlo_). Never between two verbs or after a conjugated verb.
And remember the **a** before specific people: _Visito **a** mi familia. Llamo **a** Martín._ For the person you also use the pronoun: _¿A Martín? **Lo** llamo mañana._

Dates, reasons, and invitations

**Dates**: el + number + de + month, with the month in lowercase: _el 14 de octubre_. The 1st is _el primero_ (Latin America) or _el uno_ (Spain). Ordinals for weeks and Sundays: _la primera semana de mayo_.
**Reasons**: **¿Por qué?** asks, **porque** answers, and **es que** softens an excuse: _—¿Vienes? —Lo siento, es que tengo que trabajar._

**Invitations**: invite (_¿Quieres venir a…?_), accept with energy (_¡Claro! ¡Qué buena idea!_), or decline in four steps: thanks + what a shame + es que… + another day? If it's a party, remember the intonation: the exclamation starts high and falls at the end.
In questions and suggestions: **por qué**, two words with an accent mark.

Connected sentences: linking, synalepha, clusters, and exclamations
In weeks 16–19 you worked on four features that make your Spanish sound continuous and natural. This checkpoint puts them together in real sentences.

**Linking** (week 16): the final consonant joins the next vowel: _los_amigos_ sounds "lo-sa-mi-gos." **Synalepha** (week 17): final vowel + initial vowel in one syllable: _mi_amiga_, _la_habitación_. With both, an entire sentence sounds like one long word, without breaks.

**Consonant clusters** (week 18): _tr, pr, pl, bl, cr, gr_ go together in one syllable and the r is single: **tres**, **plato**, **hablar**, never "te-res." **Exclamatory intonation** (week 19): it starts high, with energy, and falls at the end: **¡Qué buena idea!**; in lists, each item rises and only the last one falls.

Remember the variation: in the Caribbean and in Panama the final -s is aspirated and more vowels appear together; in Chile _tr_ can sound almost like _ch_; in the Río de la Plata the stressed syllable of the exclamation is stretched. All of that is correct Spanish: you choose a model and be consistent.
None of this is written: the spaces between words are still there, but they aren't heard. The only visible things are the signs **¡ !** and **¿ ?**, which tell you from the start which melody to use.

Blog post
Kenji, a Japanese student who started the course at the language exchange in Coyoacán, writes on his travel blog, in Spanish.

Hello, readers! My name is Kenji, I'm Japanese, and I've been in Panama for three months. I live in a shared apartment in El Cangrejo, on the fifth floor. It's small and a bit old, but it's very bright and close to everything. There's a living room, a kitchen, and three bedrooms. My roommates are from Colombia and Italy.

My week is intense. In the morning I have Spanish class and in the afternoon I work at a café. At home we have a list of chores: this week the kitchen is my turn. It has to be cleaned every day, because my Italian roommate cooks a lot… and very well!
This month is special: November 3 and 4 are Panama's national holidays. There are parades, music, and flags on every street. My roommates invite me to watch the parade downtown. Of course I'm going!

And afterward? In three weeks I'm going to travel to Costa Rica by bus. Before that I have to renew my visa and say goodbye to my friends. I'm going to make a Japanese dinner for them on Saturday the 21st. The menu? I'm going to decide it with them. See you soon!

What I have already experienced · forms you need

The present perfect connects an experience with the present. Form: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han + participle. With -ar verbs we use -ado; with -er and -ir verbs, -ido. The participle does not change with the person: ellas han viajado. The auxiliary and the participle are not separated by a pronoun: lo he visto.
This week I have tried a new soup.
Have you ever gone on a night hike?
Escribir has the irregular participle escrito; the auxiliary shows the person.

Ask with alguna vez without requiring a date. Ya shows that something is done; todavía leaves a possibility open; nunca denies an experience. The participles hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, puesto, vuelto, abierto, and roto are irregular. For a finished date, the preterite will appear next week. The use of the perfect varies between regions.
We have already come back, but we have not written the review yet.

The preterite presents finished actions: ayer, el sábado pasado, en 2022, or hace dos días. -ar verbs: visité, visitaste, visitó, visitamos, visitasteis, visitaron. -er/-ir verbs: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron; salí, saliste, salió, salimos, salisteis, salieron.
In the first person some letters change to keep the sound: buscar → busqué, llegar → llegué, empezar → empecé. These are spelling changes; the rest of the endings follow the regular pattern.
Yesterday I packed a backpack and left early.
On Sunday we ate by the river.
Ayer places a finished action; caminé has the stress on the last syllable.

The past forms fui, estuve, tuve, hice, pude, puse, vine, and dije are frequent. Some stems change: estar → estuv-, tener → tuv-, poder → pud-, poner → pus-, venir → vin-, decir → dij-. With them we use -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron; decir forms dijeron. Hacer has hizo in the third person.

Ver and dar have short forms without an accent mark: vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron; di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron. For example: vi un anuncio y di mi respuesta; ella vio el cartel y dio una charla.

Which neighborhood to live in? · forms you need

Compare qualities with más or menos + adjective + que and tan + adjective + como. For quantities, tanto agrees: tantas tiendas como, tanto ruido como. For actions: trabajo tanto como tú. Mejor, peor, mayor, and menor usually appear without más when they are comparatives.
This apartment is less expensive than the one downtown.
There are as many shops as in my neighborhood.
Mejor already expresses comparison.
From system to message

El más tranquilo de los barrios is a relative superlative: it needs a comparison group. Tranquilísimo intensifies a quality without comparing. In ads, distinguish facts (price, square meters, transport) from judgments (precioso, comodísimo). Your choice should connect a fact to a need; it is not enough to say something is better.

To compare city and countryside, also think about climate and services: a rural area may be quieter but have less transport; on the coast it is usually hotter than in the mountains. Avoid presenting a personal preference as a rule for everyone.
It is the brightest house of the three.
The bedroom is tiny, but the transport is better.

The direct object answers what: el libro → lo, la cámara → la, los billetes → los, las llaves → las. The indirect object shows to whom: me, te, le, nos, os, les. It goes before the direct: me lo, te la, nos los. Le and les change to se before lo, la, los, las: se lo presto.
I lend the camera to Ana; I lend it to her until Friday.
Can you lend me your charger? I'll give it back to you tomorrow.
Le becomes se before lo.
From system to message

With a conjugated verb, the pronouns go before it: te lo devuelvo. With an infinitive they can be attached: voy a devolvértelo; also te lo voy a devolver. Dámelo and explícaselo are useful formulas that you will study as instructions next week. If se is ambiguous, add a Marta or a mis vecinos.

Estar + gerund presents an ongoing action or a temporary situation: estoy estudiando, estamos buscando. -ar forms -ando; -er/-ir, -iendo. Leer → leyendo; pedir → pidiendo; dormir → durmiendo. Don't use this construction for every habit: trabajo los lunes describes a routine.

From the system to the message

Periphrases show phases: empezar a estudiar, acabar de llegar, volver a intentarlo, dejar de fumar, and seguir aprendiendo. After seguir comes a gerund; after empezar a, volver a, and dejar de comes an infinitive. Acabo de llegar expresses a very recent past. Connect the change to a concrete consequence.

Ir a + infinitive presents an intention or a plan: voy a reservar. The simple future can express a prediction or a promise: llegaré, tendremos. Add -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án to the infinitive. A real condition with si takes the present; the consequence can take the future.

Algo and nada refer to things; alguien and nadie, to people. With the indefinite after the verb, no is needed: no veo nada, no viene nadie. Before the verb, the negative indefinite is enough: nadie viene. Algún and ningún go before a masculine singular noun; alguna and ninguna before a feminine one.
I haven't found anything under the seat.
Has anyone seen a bag that has a red ribbon?
Before a masculine singular noun we use ningún.
From the system to the message

Que adds information about a person or thing: una bolsa que tiene dos bolsillos. Donde locates a place: la sala donde esperamos. If you don't know a word, explain shape, material, and use: es una cosa de metal que sirve para abrir botellas. In lost property, don't post unnecessary private information; give a detail that lets the object be recognized.
I don't have any receipt, but I have a photo.
I'm looking for the office where they keep lost property.
Is it yours or mine?

Stressed possessives agree with the thing possessed: el cuaderno es mío; la funda es mía; las llaves son mías. With an article they can replace the noun: el mío, la tuya, los suyos. Suyo can refer to him, her, you (usted), them, or you all (ustedes); add de Elena or de él if clarification is needed.
This box is mine; yours is at reception.
The coat is hers, Elena's; mine is a different color.
Mía agrees with mochila, not with the owner.

Last year we organized a book-swap afternoon. There was a lot of interest, but the room was small and some people couldn't find a place. Also, the notice was only on social media and several neighbors found out afterward. This year we want to improve the organization without spending more than sixty euros.

Option A: library room, forty euros for three hours, twenty chairs, projector included. It is near two bus stops and has step-free access. It is only available on Thursday from five to eight. Option B: patio of the cultural center, free, thirty chairs, no projector. It can be used on Saturday morning, but there is no covered space if it rains.

We can ask several families to lend books. Each item should have a card with an alias and the return date; no public contact details are needed. The activity should include a short presentation, time to talk, and an organized pick-up. Before confirming, we need to know how many people can come on Thursday and who can lend materials if we choose the patio.

The library manager explains that the twenty chairs are the limit of the room. Another row can't be added by the door because it must be kept clear. The projector works with the center's computer; before the activity it's a good idea to send a presentation in a simple format and test it there. There is no need to bring a screen or buy new materials. If we use this option, we can put the twenty euros left in the budget toward printing posters and cards.

A neighbor suggests adding a recommendations table: each participant writes two sentences about a book they have read and explains who might like it. To review the result, the team will keep only the number of attendees and a list of improvements for next time. At the end we'll ask whether the schedule was convenient, whether the notices arrived in time, and whether the instructions for returning the books were understood. We don't need a public list with personal information. Afterward we'll compare the Thursday responses with those of the small Saturday group. The next activity will be decided based on those two experiences, not just on the opinion of those who spoke the most at the meeting.

The past perfect combines había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían with an invariable participle. It places one event before another past event: it doesn't simply mean that something happened long ago. The imperfect sets the scene and the preterite moves the events forward.

I got to my sister's wedding with a borrowed backpack and a story nobody expected. I had prepared the trip a week ahead: I bought an early ticket and packed my suit in a small suitcase. The night before, I looked at the schedule, but I didn't open the notice the company had sent by email. I thought it was advertising and kept making dinner.

When I got to the station, the board showed that my train was leaving from another terminal. An employee explained that they had changed the departure because of roadworks. While she was pointing out the way, I heard the announcement of the last call. I ran to the platform, but the doors were already closed. I didn't miss the train by arriving late at the station; I missed it because I hadn't checked the change.

At the office they offered me a seat three hours later. A traveler who had overheard the conversation suggested sharing a taxi to the next station. Before accepting, we checked that the train stopped there. We managed to catch it, although my suitcase stayed by the counter. My sister lent me clothes and, finally, I was able to be with her. Since then I read notices in full and no longer rely only on the schedule I remember.

Form and meaning

The preterite marks completed events; the imperfect describes circumstances or habits; the past perfect presents prior events. The present perfect connects an experience to a period still open for the speaker. Its use varies between regions: don't turn today's explanation into an automatic rule.
Yesterday they rescued two hikers.

The neighbors had warned them beforehand.
The compound participle does not agree with the subject.
Organizing your communication

A news report distinguishes what happened from what a witness believes happened. Cite the source and acknowledge what you don't know. When listening to spontaneous stories you may hear pa for para; it is an informal reduction, not a form you should imitate or write in a news report.
This week we have received three notices.
What a scare! Thank goodness they arrived.
The witness said he hadn't seen the beginning.
Gender, number and noun reference

The article lets you introduce and pick up a referent: una testigo contó lo ocurrido; la testigo volvió después. Persona and víctima are grammatically feminine even when they refer to a man; testigo takes el testigo and la testigo. Keep agreement with the noun and check plurals such as ley → leyes.
Una testigo llamó; la testigo esperó al equipo. (A witness called; the witness waited for the team.)
The victim was calm: he was a neighbor from the area.
Laws and notices have different functions.

The bridge in the Molino neighborhood reopened yesterday after being closed for an afternoon. A neighbor had called the city council because one of the railings was moving. At first the news spread on social media that the bridge had collapsed. However, the photos that several users shared were of a repair from the previous year.

When the technicians arrived, there were quite a lot of people on both sides of the river. Some neighbors needed to cross to get home; others had come over out of curiosity. The police closed off access while the team inspected the structure. A shopkeeper explained that she had heard a bang, but admitted she had not seen any collapse. The technicians found a loose piece in the railing and replaced it. There were no injuries and no damage to the central section.
A witness who works near the bridge asked not to appear in the photographs. The witness agreed to explain what she had seen, but carefully separated her account from other people's comments.

This week the neighborhood association has received several questions about the safety of the route. Its spokesperson recommends checking the city's notices before sharing alarming messages. It also proposes putting up a sign with the date of each inspection. The incident shows that information can seem urgent without being accurate. The important news is not only that the bridge reopened, but that a timely call allowed a small problem to be repaired before it became a bigger one.

Form and meaning

The present subjunctive appears in wishes with ojalá, espero que and quiero que. For many forms you start from the present yo form and change the vowel: hablo → hable, como → coma, vivo → viva; tengo → tenga. Learn sea, vaya, haya, sepa and esté separately.
I hope you have a good start.
I hope you find a friendly team.
Have a great time at the celebration.
Espero que introduces a wish here.
Organizing your communication

Que te vaya bien does not describe a fact: it expresses a wish. With quiero viajar the wish and the action belong to the same person; with quiero que viajes the person who performs the action changes. Don't promise that everything will turn out well: accompany the wish with concrete help and an open question.
I want to go with you to the station.
I want you to write to me when you can.
I hope you are calm tonight.
Degree and shortening of the adjective

Before a masculine singular noun we use buen and mal: un buen comienzo, un mal día. Grande normally shortens to gran before a singular noun: una gran oportunidad. Igual de compares a quality; -ísimo intensifies with agreement and el más de compares within a group. Don't confuse intensifying with providing evidence.
I wish you a good start in this great opportunity.
I'm extremely happy; you are just as excited.
It's the most interesting project of the three.

Sara has just gotten a place and receives an offer of support. Listen first without the transcript. The voices are synthetic; they are not presented as verified regional models. Note who needs what and what is still to be confirmed.

Hi, Sara. I heard your message about the course you're starting on Monday. Congratulations on getting the place! I know you'd been waiting months for an answer and I'm really glad it has finally come.

Thanks. I'm happy, though I'm a little scared of speaking in front of the group. Everyone seems to have more experience. I want to make the most of the course, but I also want to sleep well and not spend my nights preparing every contribution.

I hope you find a comfortable pace. You don't need to show everything you know on the first day. I hope the teacher lets you introduce yourselves little by little. If it helps, we can practice your introduction on Sunday afternoon.
That would be good for me, but I'd rather not learn a speech by heart. I want to explain why I chose the course and ask how we'll work. Can you listen to me and tell me which part isn't clear?

Of course. Sounding natural matters more than saying everything perfectly. I'll listen first without interrupting and then I'll ask you two questions, as if I were a classmate. That way you also practice reacting.

Perfect. Then we'll talk on Sunday at six. Thanks for offering something so concrete. And I hope you enjoy your celebration on Saturday; I hope the weather is nice and that you can have dinner in the courtyard. For me this is a great opportunity and I'm extremely happy. That doesn't mean every day will be perfect; I hope to keep my enthusiasm even after a bad day.

Everyday-life feature
Original SpanishCue text. Read to understand the experience and the decision; then go back to the details.

Tomorrow Clara leaves the city to work for six months at a cultural center. Her friends organized a simple farewell: each person brought a card with a wish and a possible kind of help. They didn't want to give her a list of advice nobody had asked for. They wanted her to take something useful with her and to know whom to call if she needed company.

The first card said: «Espero que encuentres gente con la que puedas compartir tus ideas. Si quieres, el domingo podemos hablar por videollamada». Another friend wrote: «Que disfrutes del trabajo, pero también de los ratos libres. Te mando el contacto de una asociación que organiza paseos». Clara especially appreciated the messages that acknowledged her nerves. She was excited about traveling, though she was also worried about not knowing anyone. Hearing only “I'm sure it will be perfect” didn't help her as much as being able to talk about her doubts.

For Clara it was a great opportunity, though she didn't expect every day to be fantastic. She said she was just as excited as she was nervous and that one bad day would not define the whole experience.

At the end of the dinner, Clara read her own card to the group. She hoped they would keep meeting and tell her even the small news. She didn't want to receive only photos of big celebrations. «Ojalá sigamos compartiendo las cosas normales», she said. Before leaving they agreed on a first call, but without turning it into a weekly obligation. The farewell did not remove the sadness; it turned it into a beginning they could accompany.

Form and meaning

Te recomiendo que, es importante que and es mejor que introduce a recommendation with the subjunctive when we name another person's action. For a general recommendation, es importante descansar works. The negative imperative uses subjunctive forms: no vayas, no se preocupe, no lo hagas.
I recommend that you reserve a free afternoon.
It's important that you rest between tasks.
Don't go to bed with the computer on.
The prohibition for tú uses the subjunctive.
Organizing your communication

Useful advice starts with listening: sum up the problem before proposing a solution. Distinguish a suggestion from an urgent warning. Intonation and the reason you add can make no lo hagas sound like help or like a curt order.
Don't worry about answering today.
It's better to start with a small change.
You could let them know you need more time.

A person tells why she ends up accepting tasks that could have waited. Listen first without the transcript. The voices are synthetic; they are not presented as verified regional models. Note who needs what and what is still to be confirmed.

For several days I've been saying I'm going to rest and in the end I always accept another task. Yesterday I had finished what was urgent, but a colleague asked me to review his presentation. When I looked at the clock, it was almost midnight.

I understand. Before I give you advice, are you more worried about the number of tasks or about others thinking you don't want to collaborate? Having too much work is not the same as feeling you can never say no.
I think the second. My colleague didn't even need the presentation today. I assumed I had to answer right away. Then I got angry with myself and this morning I was exhausted.

Then I'd recommend that you first ask when they need it by. Don't promise an immediate answer without looking at your schedule. You can say: «Lo reviso mañana después de comer; si lo necesitas antes, habrá que buscar otra opción».

That seems possible to me. I don't want to stop helping, just organize myself better. I could also set aside half an hour to walk when I leave work, because right now I go straight from the office to the screen at home.

Try one of those things this week and then we'll see how it goes. You don't need to change all your habits today. If you accept something late again, note why you did it and think about which reply would have helped you at that moment.

Lucía explained that she got home tired, opened her computer to finish a report and went to bed much later than planned. She had tried to change everything at once, but she dropped the plan after two days.

The coordinator didn't tell her to quit her job. She asked what she could negotiate and what depended on her. Lucía admitted that she answered messages that could have waited until the next morning. The group recommended that she let people know her hours and prepare a short reply for non-urgent messages. A fellow participant added: «No conviertas el descanso en otra tarea que tengas que hacer perfectamente». The remark prompted a conversation about unrealistic expectations.

At the end, each participant chose a small change and a way to check whether it worked. Lucía decided to close her computer at an agreed time three days a week. If a real emergency came up, she would note what had happened instead of deciding the whole plan had failed. The workshop didn't offer medical treatment or promise to solve every problem. It offered a space to listen, try everyday adjustments and ask for help when those adjustments weren't enough.

This week's mission: Give opinions, express doubt and distinguish a statement from an evaluation.
Form and meaning

Creo que and es verdad que present information as asserted and usually take the indicative. No creo que, es posible que and dudo que introduce the subjunctive here. The choice depends on how you present the content, not on whether a news item is true in the world.
I think the news item needs a date.
I don't think that image is recent.
It's possible that part of the message is missing.
The negated opinion introduces the subjunctive in this use.
Organizing your communication

Before sharing something, identify who posted it, when and with what evidence. You can accept one part and qualify another: es verdad que facilita el contacto, pero no creo que sustituya una conversación. A reasoned opinion needs an example and can acknowledge a limitation.
It's true that the video is circulating widely.
From my point of view, it's best to wait.
It may be useful, though it doesn't prove everything.
Demonstratives and reference in discourse

Esto, eso and aquello can pick up a whole situation or statement, not just point to objects. The reader must know what they refer to: compartieron una foto sin fecha; eso causó confusión. Este aviso modifies a noun; esto works without a noun. If there are two possible antecedents, repeat the noun or rephrase.
The video has no date; that limits its usefulness.
This is what we know: the sign mentions roadworks.
These other messages do include a link.

A message appeared in the neighborhood group announcing the closure of the library for the whole winter. The headline was short and worrying, and several people shared it before opening the link. When she read the full story, Marta discovered that it referred to a library in another city. The neighborhood name matched, but the address and date were different.

Marta doesn't think the solution is to ban all messages about news. In her opinion, groups are for warning about problems and organizing help. However, she considers it important that each notice include its source. It is also possible that correct information becomes outdated: a canceled activity can be restored the next day. That is why she recommends checking both the place and the time a text refers to.

The group had confused the neighborhood name with that of another city. That, and not a decision by their library, explained the mistaken notice. Marta repeated the referent to avoid a second confusion.

Some neighbors think that asking for so many checks will mean nobody shares anything. Marta understands that concern, although she distinguishes an informal conversation from a notice that can change many people's plans. She proposes a simple rule: when there is no confirmation, write clearly that it is a doubt. The group has started using that formula. It doesn't guarantee that mistakes will disappear, but it lets readers know what has been checked and what still needs a call or a query.

Form and meaning

Me alegra que, me molesta que and me preocupa que express a reaction and take the subjunctive: me alegra que vengas. The fact may be real; the subjunctive doesn't always mean uncertainty. With the infinitive you can present an experience or activity without developing another clause: me alegra verte.

Organizing your communication

Don't reduce the infinitive to a mechanical same-subject rule with verbs like alegrar: in me alegra verte, who feels joy and who sees are interpreted from context. Learn the complete patterns. Describe the effect of a behavior and ask about the intention before accusing someone.

Possessives and personal relationships

The possessive before the noun takes no article in general use: mi amigo. After the noun it agrees with the thing possessed: una amiga mía, unos amigos nuestros. Un amigo mío introduces one among several; mi amigo can pick up one known from context. El mío avoids repeating the noun, but needs a clear referent.

Original SpanishCue text. Read to understand the experience and the decision; then go back to the details.

When Nadia was offered a job in another city, her brother responded with a question about rent. She had expected congratulations and felt a small letdown. He, on the other hand, was worried because he knew how hard it is to look for housing there. Neither explained at first what they felt: Nadia answered in few words and her brother thought she didn't want to talk about it.

Two days later they talked again. Nadia said she was glad to be able to change jobs, although she was overwhelmed by all the paperwork. She also explained that it had bothered her to receive only warnings. Her brother acknowledged that he had started with his worries without celebrating the news. «Me hace ilusión que tengas esta oportunidad», he clarified. Then he asked whether she wanted advice or simply to tell him how the interview had gone.

A friend of hers reminded her that asking for support doesn't mean losing independence. Nadia compared that message with her brother's: his started with precautions, which is why it had felt colder to her.

The conversation did not settle the rent, but it did settle the misunderstanding. They agreed to separate two moments: first share the news and then go over the practical matters. Nadia understood that a question could express interest even if it wasn't the reaction she expected. Her brother understood that helping doesn't always mean anticipating problems. Since then, when one of them shares something important, the other usually asks what they need at that moment. It isn't a perfect formula, but it lets them avoid some arguments and take better care of a relationship in which both trust each other.

Form and meaning

A relative clause with the indicative describes a known referent: tengo una habitación que recibe luz. With the subjunctive we present a sought characteristic without asserting that such a referent exists: busco una habitación que reciba luz. The difference is one of perspective, not of size or importance.

Organizing your communication

Quien can refer to people, donde to places and lo que to content: lo que necesito es silencio. El que and la que let you pick up a known noun. Commas and pauses mark off additional information; without them a relative clause may select only part of the group.

Quantifiers and negation in searches

Alguno and ninguno shorten before a masculine singular noun: algún piso, ningún requisito. Cualquiera becomes cualquier before a singular noun: cualquier persona. After the verb, nadie and ninguno usually need no: no conozco ninguno. Bastante and demasiado agree when they quantify nouns; demasiado doesn't change if it modifies an adjective.

Article and community experience
Original SpanishCue text. Read to understand the experience and the decision; then go back to the details.

Three students are looking for an apartment for next school year and have prepared a list that takes up almost a page. They want a place that is near downtown, that has big rooms and that isn't expensive. When they start comparing listings, they discover that no option meets all the conditions. The discussion isn't just about choosing a building; they also need to decide how they want to live together.

Julia cares about having a desk where she can study at night. Omar works from home some days and needs a stable connection. Teresa is concerned about the commute, because she leaves early for her internship. The apartment they saw on Tuesday has good rooms, but is far from public transport. The one they visited on Thursday is smaller and costs a little more, but lets each of them get to their activities without depending on the others.

They don't rule out just any apartment over a minor detail, but they won't accept just any condition either. There are quite a few incomplete listings and some prices are too high for their budget. They will ask before paying any deposit.

Instead of voting right away, they separate the essential conditions from the preferences. They discover that the courtyard, which at first seemed fundamental, matters less than quiet and communication with the owner. They also draft three rules on cleaning, visitors and expenses. They haven't signed the contract yet: they want to ask about the deposit and check the condition of the installations. Looking for an ideal apartment has helped them recognize that a workable shared life needs more concrete agreements than a pretty photograph.

Form and meaning

The simple conditional is formed with the infinitive plus the endings ía, ías, ía, íamos, íais, ían; there are stems such as tendría, podría, haría and diría. It is used to ask politely and to advise: ¿podría aclararlo?, yo en tu lugar preguntaría. It doesn't always express a condition.
Could you explain how the shifts are organized?
I would like to work in customer service.
In your place, I would prepare a concrete example.
A present hypothetical wish is expressed.
Organizing your communication

The future can express a present conjecture: estará en una reunión. The conditional allows a conjecture about a past moment: serían las cinco. A lo mejor usually takes the indicative; quizás and tal vez let you present different degrees of commitment. Always signal what you know and what you suppose.
She isn't answering: she must be in an interview.
When he called, it must have been nine.
Maybe they've changed the schedule.

Article and community experience
Original SpanishCue text. Read to understand the experience and the decision; then go back to the details.

At the end of an interview, Alicia was convinced they wouldn't hire her. The conversation had lasted less than she expected and the manager hadn't explained when they would make the decision. On the way home, she remembered each answer and began to imagine mistakes. «A lo mejor necesitaban a alguien con más experiencia», she thought. However, she had no information confirming that explanation.

Her brother suggested reviewing the conversation by separating facts from hypotheses. Alicia had described a problem she solved in her previous job and had asked about the shifts. The manager had taken notes and had asked for her availability for a second meeting. Those were facts. That she seemed serious or looked at the clock allowed several interpretations: maybe she had another appointment or was following a tight schedule. It didn't tell her the outcome.

Alicia decided to write a short message to thank them for the interview and ask when she would hear back. She didn't want to demand an immediate answer or apologize for imaginary mistakes. Two days later she received an invitation to meet the team. She then found out that the manager had had to leave early for a meeting. The experience taught her to prepare clear examples, ask politely and avoid turning an impression into a certainty before having enough information.

Form and meaning

A collective decision combines statements, evaluations and searches: sabemos que el local cierra temprano; nos preocupa que falte espacio; buscamos uno que abra más tarde. Before selecting the mood, identify the intention each construction expresses.

Form and meaning

Cuando, en cuanto and hasta que take the indicative when they present habits or facts: cuando llego, llamo. For a pending future event they use the subjunctive: cuando llegue, llamaré. Antes de que introduces the subjunctive; antes de salir uses the infinitive when you don't need another clause.
When we receive the answer, we'll book the room.
When we receive a request, we send a notice.
As soon as the design is finished, I'll send it to you.
The future time clause uses the present subjunctive.
Organizing communication

A useful plan distinguishes fixed date, time condition, and person responsible. Don't confuse cuando llegue la autorización with si llega: the first organizes the timing; the second poses a condition. Summarize dependencies so another person knows what they can do now and what they must wait for.
We'll wait until the office opens.
Before the guests arrive, check the chairs.
I'm going to go check the entrance.

Form and meaning

Para plus infinitive expresses purpose when the action is presented with no other subject: llevo una botella para ahorrar envases. Para que plus subjunctive develops another action: ponemos una fuente para que todos rellenen sus botellas. Por usually introduces a cause; para here indicates the goal.
We install containers to sort the waste.
We put up signs so that nobody mixes up the containers.
Since information was missing, we held a meeting.
Purpose with para que uses the subjunctive.
Organizing communication

Porque explains the cause after the main idea; como usually comes before it: como falta sombra, plantaremos árboles. Ya que presents a shared reason, and es que can justify an oral answer. Don't promise absolute results: explain what will change, for whom, and how it will be checked.

Por fin expresses that something expected has arrived; para nada reinforces a negation; por si acaso prepares for a possibility. Estoy por llamar here expresses an inclination to do it. Don't translate por and para as a single relationship: interpret the whole expression.
Since we're using the courtyard, let's take care of its plants too.
I'm bringing a bag just in case it's needed.
We finally found a solution; it wasn't easy at all.

We want to propose a water fountain at the sports center so that people can refill their bottles. Right now many people buy a drink every time they come, and then the containers end up in the courtyard trash cans.

The idea seems interesting to me, but I'd like to understand the cost. Since the budget is small, we have to explain why this measure should have priority over others. Have you asked how many people would use the fountain?

We ran a survey over three afternoons. Quite a few users said they would bring a bottle if they could fill it here. We can't guarantee that everyone will change their habits, but we can offer an option that doesn't exist now.

Then it would be a good idea to add a clear sign and check on maintenance. There's no point installing something if afterward nobody knows whether the water is available. We also need to decide who will report when there is a problem.

The front desk can log the reports, and the maintenance team can review the fountain along with the rest of the facilities. We propose observing its use for two months, to see whether the number of containers drops and whether difficulties appear.

With that information I can present the proposal. I'll also bring the maintenance estimate in case they ask. A plan with people responsible and a review convinces me more than a promise to eliminate all waste at once.

At the neighborhood market, a lot of small bags were thrown away at the end of each morning. An association proposed banning them immediately, but several vendors pointed out that some people needed to separate wet products. Since they didn't want to replace one problem with another, they began by observing when the bags were used and what alternatives were possible.

The final campaign combined three measures. They put up a sign so customers would remember to bring containers, offered reused boxes for large purchases, and set aside bags for products that really needed them. A week before the start, they explained the changes at each stall. They didn't do it to give a perfect image of the market, but to reduce one specific kind of waste without making shopping harder for those with fewer options.

After a month they counted how many bags had been handed out and asked vendors and customers what had worked. Use had dropped, although some signs weren't well understood. They decided to add drawings and place them before the checkout area. The campaign did not solve all of the neighborhood's environmental problems; it made it possible to test a small change and improve it. For its organizers, that result was more useful than announcing a big transformation without explaining what each person should do on arriving at the market.

The next day, a neighbor thanked her for the precision. He had understood that the elevator would be out of service all week, but the notice said it would be closed only for some hours and that the schedules would be announced later. Paula realized that summarizing doesn't mean cutting words at random. You have to keep the conditions that change what a person can do with the information. Since then, when taking notes, she marks with a symbol the doubts she needs to confirm before becoming the group's messenger.

Amina started volunteering at a community library and during the first week wrote down several questions. She didn't understand why some people went straight into the meeting room and others waited by the front desk. At first she thought there was a rule nobody had explained to her. Later she discovered that it depended on the activity: groups with a reservation could go in, while new visitors had to ask where each inquiry was handled.

The coordinator decided to prepare a short guide with the team. They avoided phrases like «aquí todo el mundo sabe» and described concrete situations. Books are lent for two weeks; silence is requested in the small room; talking is allowed in the workshops. The guide also clarifies that the main door is closed during the break, although the building stays open through the side entrance. That is an important difference for someone arriving for the first time.
The volunteers help one another during setup. Each person organizes themselves before opening, but when a doubt comes up, a common answer is sought so as not to give contradictory instructions.

Amina added a recommendation: when someone doesn't understand an instruction, it's better to rephrase it than to automatically speak louder. An unfamiliar word or a fast pace doesn't mean lack of attention. The library began to use examples and to point out the spaces while explaining. The new guide didn't claim to represent the customs of a whole city. It recorded agreements from one specific place and reminded people that anyone could ask about their meaning or propose an improvement.

It's been a year since I changed careers, and it still surprises me to say it. I worked in a shop, but I'd been thinking for a while about going into bicycle repair. It wasn't a decision made in one afternoon: first I took a course while I kept working.

And how did you feel when you started? I imagine you already knew how to deal with customers, although learning a new trade requires accepting that some things go slowly and that you have to ask a lot of questions.

I got nervous the first time I had a bicycle in front of me without the instructor. I froze for a few minutes. Then I went over my notes and asked for help. Over time I've become less impatient; now I check each step instead of rushing to look like an expert.
Have you been at the same shop the whole year, or have you been through several places? I'm also interested in what helped you stick with the decision when the first difficulties came up.

I've been at this shop for seven months. I depend on the team's collaboration, and I trust my colleagues to recognize what I still don't know. I dream of opening a place of my own someday, but I don't want to do it before I have enough experience.

I think it's valuable that you tell that part too. Sometimes we only hear the final result and forget the transition. Your story shows that changing can include enthusiasm and doubts at the same time, without one emotion canceling the other. I keep learning every day and I've stopped pretending I know everything. Recently I went back over my first notes; I've just started a repair that used to seem impossible to me.

Sergio has lived in Puebla for eight months. He moved to work at a small company, and at first he thought the adjustment would be over once he learned the way to the office. However, he soon found out that knowing a city isn't only about finding your way around. He missed simple conversations, places where people recognized him, and activities that didn't depend on work.

During the first weeks he got nervous every time he had to ask for clarification. He would stay quiet so as not to look lost and then make mistakes he could have avoided. A coworker told him she had also been through a move. She recommended that he choose a regular activity and accept that feeling part of a place takes time. Sergio went back to a drawing workshop and began volunteering at a library on Saturdays.
Sergio keeps learning the team's customs and has stopped treating every doubt as a failure. He has started drawing regularly again and has just offered to organize a small show of the workshop.

He has now been taking part in the workshop for five months and has become more patient with his own progress. He doesn't think every move is a wonderful adventure or that difficulties disappear just because you have a good attitude. He still misses his friends and depends on complicated schedules to call them. But he has learned to keep those ties while he builds others. When someone new joins the team, he remembers his first day and offers a concrete explanation before assuming that person already knows how everything works.

Original SpanishCue text. Read to understand the experience and the decision; then go back to the details.

An association received an unexpected offer: it could use a space free of charge for a year, but it had to take care of small repairs and open it to the neighborhood two afternoons a week. At the first meeting, some immediately imagined workshops, exhibitions, and a library of objects. Others remembered that the group already had trouble dividing up its current tasks.

The coordinator proposed discussing a different question: «Si aceptáramos, ¿qué dejaríamos de hacer?». She didn't want to dampen the enthusiasm, but to relate it to the available time. If everyone could contribute four more hours, the project would be simple; in reality, many people worked or cared for relatives. One participant suggested sharing the space with another association. That would reduce the work, although it would require negotiating schedules and storage.

The group drew up two scenarios. In the first they accepted the whole space and suspended one monthly activity. In the second they proposed using it just one afternoon, with a smaller commitment. Neither option was perfect. They decided to ask the owner whether he would accept a three-month trial before committing for a year. Imagining possibilities let them discover desires, but also limits. The final question stopped being «¿nos gustaría tener un local?» and became «¿qué proyecto podemos sostener sin agotar a quienes lo hacen posible?».

Sin embargo and en cambio link contrasting ideas; además adds an argument. Aunque with the indicative acknowledges a fact that doesn't prevent the conclusion: aunque es cómodo, exige organización. Por un lado and por otro help compare aspects, but each side needs concrete content.

Aunque already introduces the concession; pero is not added in this construction.

A short opinion text presents a position, develops reasons with examples, and closes without repeating everything word for word. You can defend a preference and admit an exception. Before writing, distinguish a personal experience from a claim about everyone who learns.

By contrast, my classmate learns better with short meetings.

Two students compare the conditions in which they are able to learn. Listen first without the transcript. The voices are synthetic; they are not presented as verified regional models. Note who needs what and what remains to be confirmed.

Studying online has worked for me because I work some Saturdays. Before, I would miss class and then find it hard to keep up. Now I can go over the materials another day and prepare questions for the tutoring session.

I understand that advantage. In my case, though, home isn't always a quiet place. I share a room and sometimes I end up staring at the screen without concentrating. That's why I prefer to have a place to go to.

Maybe the problem isn't choosing one format for everything. Although I study remotely, I also need to talk with other people. I'd like there to be short meetings to practice, without forcing us to travel every week.

That could work. Also, the center could open a study room for those of us who don't have good conditions at home. That way the materials would stay flexible, but we wouldn't depend only on our personal resources.

Good idea. On one hand we'd keep the freedom of schedule; on the other we'd have support and contact. We'd need to ask how many people would use that room and at what times, so as not to open it when nobody can come.

So our proposal isn't to claim that digital or in-person is always better. It's to combine what helps people learn and then check whether people take part. We can bring two concrete examples to the meeting so it doesn't stay as an opinion that's too general.

At the training center they are debating whether the next course should be entirely online. Those who support the proposal point out that many people take an hour to get there and that digital materials let you repeat an explanation. Also, some of the students work irregular hours. For that group, being able to study at different times is not a luxury but the condition that makes it possible to follow the course.

However, others remind us that having access to a video does not guarantee learning. Some share housing and can't find a quiet place. Others need to ask questions while they practice. The teacher of a technical workshop explains that she usually discovers a difficulty by watching how someone uses a tool. That information doesn't always show up in a questionnaire. Although she values digital resources, she believes certain activities require presence and support.

My preference would be to combine materials that each person can go over at their own pace with regular meetings to practice and resolve doubts. I wouldn't propose the same combination for every course. In a hands-on workshop more in-person sessions would be needed; in a reading course, short meetings might be enough. What matters is deciding what the activity needs and checking who is left out of each format. Choosing solely on cost or technological novelty can hide the real conditions in which students study.

I prefer a course that combines individual work with practice meetings. On the one hand, going over materials at my own pace lets me stop at what I don't understand and repeat an explanation.

For example, I can prepare a reading on my own and then bring my questions to a tutoring session. By contrast, when I rehearse a conversation, I need answers I don't know in advance. That difference between activities seems more useful to me than defending one format for every situation.

Also, I can organize my study when my schedule changes. On the other hand, I need to talk and get feedback on what I produce. A video doesn't always help me discover why an answer is unclear. Although in-person classes make that exchange easier, traveling every day can be hard for people who live far away. That is why I would propose materials that are accessible during the week and a regular session to practice with other people. I don't think this arrangement works equally well for all subjects. We would need to check which activities require being present and ask students what conditions they need in order to really take part.

Form and meaning

A semi-formal complaint organizes identification of the service, facts, effect, and request. The conditional softens without removing clarity: quisiera solicitar un cambio. Keep usted in a formal relationship and avoid mixing forms. A proposed date for receiving a reply is not the same as inventing a legal right.
I would like to request a review of the reservation.
I would appreciate it if you would confirm the new date.
The service received does not match what was advertised.

Mediating a conflict means summarizing the needs of both parties without deciding for them. Rephrase an accusation as a specific problem, ask what solution they would accept, and confirm the agreement. If a personal relationship is involved, separate the discomfort from the facts of the service.

Good morning. I'm calling about the room reservation for last Thursday. The number ends in four, seven, two. The confirmation listed an internet connection, but it wasn't available and we had to change our activity.

Thank you for explaining. To check it, can you confirm whether the reservation was from five to seven in the afternoon? I see an incident that day, although I need to make sure I'm reviewing the same service.

Yes, that was the time. I appreciate that you offered us another room, but it was too small for the group. I would like to know whether you can refund part of the amount or propose a compensation we can use later.

I can request a partial refund. I don't want to promise an amount before the manager reviews the case. I'll send you a summary today and tomorrow we'll confirm the proposal to you in writing. Does that timeframe suit you?

Yes, thank you. I would appreciate it if the summary stated that we held the activity without the advertised connection. We are not claiming for a complete cancellation. I would also like it to be clear that we appreciate the front desk's help.

I'll note it that way. Let me repeat the number to confirm: four, seven, two. You'll receive the summary today and the reply tomorrow. If it doesn't arrive, you can reply to the same message with that reference, without explaining the whole situation again to someone else.

Original SpanishCue text. Read to understand the experience and the decision; then go back to the details.

Eva booked a room for a meeting of her association. The ad said there was a projector and internet access, but when she arrived she found that the connection wasn't working. The person at the front desk offered her another, smaller room. They could connect there, although not everyone who had signed up fit. Eva decided to hold the meeting without a digital presentation and to explain the problem afterward in writing.

Her first draft said the center never fulfilled anything. When she reviewed it, she remembered that it was the first time they had used the service and that the front desk had tried to help. She replaced the general accusation with the facts: date, reservation number, advertised condition, and the difficulty encountered. She attached the receipt and asked for a partial refund or an equivalent discount for another activity. She also asked them to confirm when they could reply, without presenting her preference as a legal obligation.

The manager called to review the case. She explained that the breakdown had started that morning and acknowledged that they should have warned them earlier. She offered a partial refund and a written confirmation. In the association, a colleague was still angry because he had recommended the center and felt he was being blamed. Eva clarified that they were complaining about a service, not about his advice. Solving the problem required handling two different conversations: one about the reservation and another about trust within the group.

The neighborhood repair workshop ends its first quarter with a mixed review. Thirty people took part at least once, and several objects their owners had been about to throw away were recovered. Negotiating responsibilities in a team

Noun clauses present information or an action that someone influences. Stating, checking, or perceiving normally introduces the indicative; asking, evaluating, or denying a statement usually introduces the subjunctive. Looking for que is not enough: you have to interpret what the speaker is doing with the message.
Marta states that the team is ready.
A statement is being presented.
Marta demands that the team hand in the report.
Demanding influences another person.
She reminds us to attend tomorrow; it is a call to meet.
Here, reminding conveys a request.
Demanding selects the subjunctive when it influences a different subject.
Interpretation, register, and effect

Saying, insisting, and reminding allow two interpretations: she reports that the date is firm, but she tells us to hand in the draft. With different subjects, que and a conjugated verb appear; with the same subject, quiero revisar. An indirect request still needs someone responsible, a deadline, and a real possibility of a response.

Team: after Monday's meeting, I want to clarify what was decided and what is still pending. The client confirms that the presentation will be on Friday; he has not asked us to finish all the tests by then. That difference matters. If we promise a final version, the technical team will have to work at night and, even so, will not be able to guarantee that it works on all devices. I propose that we show a prototype and explain its limits clearly. I don't consider it acceptable to pass on to the client a certainty that we don't yet have.

Lucía insists that she has two people available to review the data. Tomás, on the other hand, insists that we assign a third person to design. Both statements seem incompatible only if we assume that all tasks must be done at the same time. I suggest that Lucía finish the figures first and that Tomás get support afterward. I need each person responsible to say, before Wednesday, what they can deliver without compromising quality. No one has to justify their personal circumstances publicly; it is enough to state their availability and the dependencies of their work.

It is also worth reviewing how we ask for help. During the meeting it was repeated that the team should get more involved, but it was not specified who would do what. An invitation that general can seem kind and turn out to be of little use. I prefer a precise request that allows negotiation to a demand disguised as enthusiasm. For my part, I will handle the conversation with the client and communicate any change of scope. I ask you not to accept new tasks without first checking their effect on the deadlines already agreed.

On Thursday we will check progress. If a blocker appears, we will record it together with an alternative, without looking for someone to blame. The aim of this email is to distribute decisions as well as work: coordinating well does not mean being available at all hours, but knowing what each person expects and what they can expect from the others.

When his daughter announced that she wanted to dedicate herself to restoring musical instruments, Ernesto reacted with a question: «And what are you going to live on?». Clara heard a prohibition, although her father never told her to give it up. For months they argued over a sentence whose meaning both believed to be obvious. He expected her to draw up a plan; she needed him to recognize the seriousness of a choice she had been preparing for years. The conversation did not move forward until they stopped defending words and began explaining concerns.

Ernesto had grown up in a family for whom having a stable job was a recent achievement. His parents wanted him to study a degree that would let him become independent soon. They did not demand that he become a lawyer, but they celebrated his choice as if he had solved all the family's problems forever. Now he understands that he passed that same pressure on to his daughter, even though he used seemingly more open language. Saying that everyone can do what they want does not eliminate the expectations communicated through silences, jokes, or comparisons.

Clara, for her part, admits that she interpreted any doubt as a put-down. She had researched schools and workshops, but she had not calculated how much it would cost to support herself during the training. It bothered her to be treated as if she were still a child; yet when they asked her for concrete details, she answered that no one trusted her. An aunt stepped in without deciding who was right. She asked each of them to summarize the other's concern before formulating a response.

They did not end up thinking the same. Ernesto still considers the profession risky and Clara keeps her project. They agreed to review a budget together and limit family help to a defined period. The change was more modest than a movie-style reconciliation: they learned to disagree without turning every disagreement into a test of affection. For both of them, that was a fairly concrete form of respect.

I propose resuming the conversation with a rule: before responding, each person will summarize the other's concern and ask whether they have understood it. It does let us tell a reasonable warning from an expectation that perhaps needs revising.

I would also like to own my part: I researched schools, but I avoided calculating some expenses because I feared they would weaken my argument. Presenting them clearly does not mean giving up the project. It means defending it with information and accepting that autonomy includes taking on its difficulties.

For me it has been useful for reviewing how I congratulate people. Before, I used to say that everything had gone perfectly. Now I prefer to point out what I value and ask what should be improved. It's less glossy, perhaps, but it allows a more honest conversation about the library's future.
